q: A claims team processes each submitted form the same way every time: extract the fields, check them against policy rules in code, then draft a decision letter. Auditors want identical steps on every run. Which design BEST fits?
opts: A prompt chain with a code-based validation gate between extraction and drafting
A single autonomous agent given every internal tool and told to use its own judgment each run
An orchestrator that invents a different set of worker tasks for each form it receives
A pair of cooperating agents that debate the decision until both of them agree on it
why: When the steps are known in advance and must be repeatable, a workflow with fixed code paths is the right tool. A prompt chain keeps each model call small and lets code verify the intermediate result before the next step. An autonomous agent chooses its own path, which defeats the audit requirement. Dynamic orchestration and agent debate add variability and cost without any benefit here.

q: An engineering team wants to hand Claude open-ended tickets such as "the nightly export is slow". The number and kind of investigative steps cannot be known up front, and results depend on what each command returns. What is the MOST appropriate architecture?
opts: One large prompt that lists every possible diagnostic command to run in a fixed order
An agent loop that picks each next step from tool results, with turn and budget caps
A fixed three-step prompt chain that diagnoses the slowdown, proposes a fix and summarises it
A router that classifies the ticket once and replies with a canned template for that category
why: Open-ended problems where each action depends on the last observation are the case for an agent: the model plans, calls tools, reads results and adapts. Because the path is unpredictable, set max turns and a budget so cost stays bounded. A fixed chain, canned routing or a scripted command list assume a path that the problem does not have.

q: A modernization project must update an unknown number of modules; which files change only becomes clear after reading the codebase. Each module change is independent once identified. Which pattern fits BEST?
opts: Sectioning: split the repository into five equal folders in advance and run them in parallel
Orchestrator-workers: a lead call splits the work at run time and delegates to workers
Routing: classify the request once and send it to one specialist prompt for the whole change
Evaluator-optimizer: generate one patch and loop on critique until the critic is satisfied
why: The defining trait of orchestrator-workers is that the decomposition is created at run time by a central model, which matches subtasks that are unknown until the code has been read. Fixed sectioning assumes the slices are known in advance, routing handles a single choice, and evaluator-optimizer refines one output rather than fanning out work.

q: A marketing tool translates product copy and must match a written style guide precisely. Reviewers can state clear pass or fail criteria, and a second pass with feedback usually fixes the problems. Which pattern is the BEST fit?
opts: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts, another checks the criteria, with a cap on rounds
Voting: run ten independent translations and ship whichever one is the longest
Orchestrator-workers: let the model invent a new set of subtasks for every sentence
Routing: send each paragraph to a different language specialist and join the results
why: A generate-then-critique loop works when criteria are explicit and feedback demonstrably improves the draft. Cap the number of iterations so it terminates. Routing and orchestration do not address iterative quality improvement, and picking the longest of several outputs has no relationship to style-guide compliance.

q: A support assistant must reply to a customer and, separately, check the customer's message against a content policy. The check needs only the incoming message, not the reply, and latency matters. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Replace both calls with one agent that decides for itself whether any checking is needed
Ask one prompt to write the reply and check the message itself in a single response, then trust it
Run the policy check only after a human has read and approved the finished reply
Run the reply generation and a separate policy-check call at the same time, then combine in code
why: Independent subtasks can be sectioned and run in parallel, then merged by deterministic code, which saves wall-clock time and gives the policy check a dedicated prompt. A single prompt that does both jobs mixes responsibilities and is harder to test. Adding a human step or an agent decision adds delay and variability for no gain.

q: A lead agent delegates "fix the failing test" to a test-runner subagent. The subagent replies that it does not know which repository, branch or test to look at, although the lead discussed all three with the user. What is the root cause?
opts: Subagents need a higher turn limit before they are able to recall earlier messages
The subagent runs on a model that is too small to be able to read the repository
The user is required to repeat all of the details directly to every subagent
A subagent starts with a fresh context, so the task prompt must carry those details
why: Subagents do not inherit the parent conversation; the only channel is the task prompt the parent writes. Put file paths, errors and decisions into that prompt. Model size, repeating the user's message and raising turn limits do not give the subagent information it was never sent.

q: One agent with 40 tools spanning billing, shipping, returns and fraud frequently chooses the wrong tool and its context fills quickly. Which change is MOST likely to help?
opts: Remove the tool descriptions entirely in order to save tokens in every request
Increase the maximum number of turns so the agent has more chances to recover from errors
Add a much longer system prompt that lists all 40 tools again, each in great detail
Split into specialist subagents with focused tool sets, coordinated by a lead agent
why: Specialists with narrow toolsets reduce selection errors and keep each context focused, while the lead only routes work and merges reports. Repeating tool lists costs more context, more turns just allows more mistakes, and removing descriptions makes tool selection worse.

q: An overnight agent given the prompt "improve the codebase" ran for hours and produced a large bill. Which change BEST prevents a repeat?
opts: Tell the agent in the prompt that it should be very careful about how much it spends
Set turn and spend limits, and give a scoped goal with clear completion criteria
Switch to a different model that is guaranteed never to call any tools at all
Lower the sampling temperature so that the agent makes fewer decisions overall
why: Open-ended goals need hard stops. Turn and budget limits are enforced by the harness regardless of what the model decides, and a scoped goal tells it when to finish. A prompt reminder is advisory, temperature does not bound work, and removing tool use turns the agent into a different system altogether.

q: A custom loop built on the Messages API lets Claude call a delete_record tool. Security requires that deletions on the production database can never run without a ticket number. Which control is BEST?
opts: Add "never delete without a ticket" to the system prompt and write it in capital letters
Check for the ticket in the code that dispatches the tool call and reject calls without one
Ask Claude at the end of every run whether it happened to delete anything without a ticket
Rely on the model's own refusal behavior to stop any destructive action from happening
why: A rule that must always hold belongs in code that executes outside the model: the dispatcher checks the precondition and returns an error result when it is missing. Prompt wording only makes compliance likely, after-the-fact self-reporting cannot prevent damage, and refusal behavior is not a substitute for authorization checks.

q: An agent drafts refunds. Refunds above a set amount must be approved by a person before the payment tool runs. Where should the approval gate live?
opts: In the harness, pausing before the payment tool executes and resuming only on approval
In the tool description, written as a request that someone approve each payment first
In the system prompt, as an instruction to politely ask a person before paying anything
In a post-run email that reports every payment after the payments have already happened
why: Human-in-the-loop approval must be enforced by the loop or a permission callback so the tool cannot run until a person decides. Prompt text and tool descriptions are guidance the model could skip, and reporting after the fact is too late to stop a payment.

q: A company wants researchers to start multi-hour analysis tasks that read files, run code and browse, then check back later. The team does not want to build a loop, sandbox or tool executor. What is the BEST fit?
opts: A synchronous Messages API call that sets a very large max_tokens value for the task
The Message Batches API, because the tasks are long and do not need an instant answer
Claude Managed Agents, which hosts the harness and sandbox and streams session events
A prompt chain running inside a web server request handler while the user waits
why: Managed Agents provides the agent loop, tool execution and a sandbox, with stateful sessions suited to long-running asynchronous work. A single synchronous call cannot run tools, the Batches API processes independent Messages requests rather than an agent loop, and tying work to a web request invites timeouts.

q: A hospital group likes the Managed Agents harness but requires that file access and tool execution stay inside its own network. Which option BEST satisfies this?
opts: A self-hosted sandbox environment served by a worker that the hospital runs itself
A prompt chain in the Messages API with the sensitive files pasted into the messages
The default Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox plus a firewall note written into the prompt
A system prompt asking the agent to avoid sending any sensitive data out of the network
why: A self-hosted environment keeps tool execution, files and network egress on infrastructure the customer controls, while orchestration stays on Anthropic's side. Tool inputs and results still flow to Anthropic so the model can see them, which the team should confirm is acceptable. A prompt note is not a control, and pasting files into prompts sends them out anyway.

q: An Agent SDK run ends and the code prints result.result, but sometimes the field is missing and the job crashes. The logs show some runs stopped after 30 turns. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Check the result message's subtype first; on a turn-limit stop, resume or report progress
Wrap the print in a try block and quietly ignore the failure whenever the field is absent
Remove the turn limit completely so that every single run is able to finish on its own
Retry the same query again from scratch up to three times before giving up on the task
why: The final message carries the result text only when the subtype is success; limit and error subtypes have no result field. Handle each subtype deliberately, and use the session ID to resume after a turn limit. Silencing the error hides the problem, removing the limit invites runaway cost, and blind restarts repeat the same work.

q: A team writes a Messages API agent whose file-writing tool must be shown to a reviewer, with the reviewer's decision logged, before it runs. Which implementation approach fits BEST?
opts: A longer prompt that tells Claude to wait for the reviewer before it writes any file
Two separate API calls, one to plan the change and one to write it without any checks
The automatic tool runner, with the write tool marked as safe so that it runs unattended
A manual loop that pauses on the tool_use block, records the decision, then returns the result
why: When you need an approval gate or custom logging around a tool call, own the loop: stop at the tool_use block, run the review, then send the tool_result or an error result. The automatic tool runner is for cases without such interception, and a prompt cannot make the process wait for a human.

q: A response arrives with stop_reason tool_use and contains two tool_use blocks with different IDs. What must the next request contain?
opts: A user message with a plain text summary of what the two tools happened to find
The history plus one user message holding a tool_result per ID, with the results first
An assistant message containing both results so that the model sees them as its own words
Only the result of the first tool, because the second one will simply be requested again
why: Every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result, returned in a user message that immediately follows the assistant turn, with the result blocks before any text. Leaving one out or answering with prose breaks the pairing and produces a 400 error; results are never sent as assistant messages.

q: Developers put "never modify .env files" in CLAUDE.md, but an Agent SDK agent occasionally edits one. What is the MOST reliable remedy?
opts: A PreToolUse hook that denies Write and Edit calls aimed at .env files
Repeating the rule three more times in CLAUDE.md and adding strong emphasis to it
Asking the agent to confirm at the end of the run that it left every .env file alone
Moving the rule into the very first message of each new session instead of the file
why: CLAUDE.md is loaded as context, not enforced configuration, so the model usually but not always follows it. A PreToolUse hook runs in your process before the tool executes and can deny the call every time. Emphasis, end-of-run confirmation and relocating the text are all still guidance.

q: During a very long agent run, the agent starts ignoring a formatting rule that was given only in the first user message. The SDK reported a compaction earlier. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Increase the sampling temperature so that the model explores a wider range of behaviors
Disable all of the tools so that the context window can no longer keep on growing
Ask the user to repeat the formatting rule by hand roughly every ten turns of the run
Move the persistent rule into CLAUDE.md or the system prompt, which are sent on every request
why: Compaction summarises older turns, so a detail that existed only in early conversation can be lost. Content in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md is re-injected on every request and survives. Temperature does not restore lost context, disabling tools removes the point of the agent, and manual repetition is brittle.

q: A security-review subagent should read and search code but must never change files. How should it be defined?
opts: Give it a restricted tool list with only read-oriented tools such as Read, Grep and Glob
Write "do not edit files" in its prompt while still giving it every available tool
Run it under the permission mode that skips all permission prompts for convenience
Let it inherit all of the parent's tools and rely on a code review of its output later
why: Limiting the subagent's tools removes the capability instead of asking the model not to use it, which is a structural guarantee. A prompt instruction alone, inheriting every tool or skipping permission prompts all leave the write tools reachable.

q: A team needs a multi-step approval process that can pause for days, resume from saved state, and branch explicitly between deterministic checks and model-driven steps. Which choice BEST matches this need?
opts: A single long Messages API request that is kept open until the approver finally replies
A one-shot prompt that describes the whole approval process in prose and nothing else
A graph-based orchestration framework such as LangGraph, with durable state and interrupts
A prompt chain with no storage that restarts from the very top after each long pause
why: Durable execution, persisted state and explicit graph branching are what graph-based orchestration frameworks provide. A held-open request will time out, prose cannot persist state, and restarting from the top loses the progress that a resumable design keeps.

q: A developer new to agents must ship a feature in a week that gives Claude two simple tools. Which starting point is the BEST choice?
opts: Avoid tools completely and parse the model's prose with regular expressions instead
Write a small tool loop, or use the SDK tool runner, and add a framework later if needed
Adopt the largest multi-agent framework available so that the design is future-proof
Build a supervisor agent with five specialist subagents even though there are two tools
why: For a narrow problem, the simplest design that works is best: a short loop or the SDK helper is easy to test and debug, and a framework can be adopted later if complexity appears. Large frameworks and multi-agent hierarchies add abstraction and cost up front, and regex-parsing prose is the fragile approach that tool use exists to avoid.

q: Claude returns three tool_use blocks in one reply. Two tools succeed and the third times out. How should the harness respond in the next request?
opts: Send all three results, marking the failed one with an error flag and a clear message
Send only the two successful results and hope that the model quietly ignores the third
Retry the timed-out tool without any limit before replying to the model at all
Abort the whole conversation and simply tell the user that the request has failed
why: Every tool_use ID must be answered. Returning an error result with a clear message lets the model adapt, for example retry, try another tool or tell the user. Omitting a result is invalid, aborting wastes the successful work, and an unbounded retry can hang the agent.

q: An assistant should remember a user's preferences across weeks and many separate sessions without keeping every old transcript in context. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Telling the user to paste their saved preferences into the chat at the start each time
A persistent memory store the agent reads and writes, loaded selectively into new sessions
Raising max_tokens so that every single reply can carry a great deal more history along
Resending the complete transcript of every past session with each and every new call
why: Persistent memory lives outside the context window and can be read on demand, so only relevant facts are loaded. Larger output caps do not store anything, replaying all history wastes context and cost and will eventually not fit, and pushing the work onto the user defeats the feature.

q: A lead agent fans out to eight parallel subagents for a review and the bill is higher than expected. Which control directly addresses overall spend in the Agent SDK?
opts: A lower sampling temperature configured on each one of the subagents
A maximum budget option, whose total includes the subagents' spend
A shorter description text written on each individual subagent definition
Asking every subagent to reply in fewer words whenever it reports back
why: The spend cap covers the whole run, subagents included, and stops the loop when estimated spend reaches the limit. Remember it can overshoot by about one response. Temperature and description length do not bound spend, and brevity requests only trim output.

q: A compliance process must execute exactly the same ordered checks on every record, and a regulator will inspect the code path. A teammate proposes a prompt telling an agent to "always follow these seven steps". What is the BEST response?
opts: Switch to a bigger model, since a larger model is certain to follow the order exactly
Accept the proposal, because a clearly written prompt is enough to guarantee the order
Let the agent decide the order for itself, and simply log afterwards what it did
Put the seven steps in code and call the model only where language skills are needed
why: Where a fixed, inspectable order is a requirement, put the control flow in code and use the model for bounded sub-tasks. A prompt makes the order likely, not certain, logging after the fact does not enforce it, and model size does not turn guidance into a guarantee.

q: An agent keeps calling the same search tool with nearly identical queries and never converges. Which combination of changes is MOST appropriate?
opts: Increase max_tokens so that each individual search reply can be much longer than before
Remove the search tool and ask the model to answer from its own memory instead of searching
Raise the retry count that is used for transient API errors on every call to the API
Add a turn cap, a clear completion criterion and an explicit "no more results" tool reply
why: Loops need hard stops and clear signals. A turn cap bounds the damage, a stated completion criterion tells the model when it is done, and informative tool results let it conclude. Removing the tool abandons the task, longer replies do not break a loop, and API-error retries are unrelated.

q: In Managed Agents, a task requires auditing hundreds of independent documents quickly and merging the findings. Which capability is the BEST match?
opts: A dynamic workflow where the agent writes a program that fans out many agents
A much larger system prompt that lists every document the agent needs to read in turn
An advisor model that the agent consults after it finishes reading each single page
A single subagent that is asked to read every one of the documents one after another
why: Dynamic workflows let the agent write a program that runs many agents in parallel phases and combines their outputs, which fits work with many independent pieces. Every agent spends tokens, so a budget caps cost. One sequential subagent is slow, an advisor adds guidance rather than parallel capacity, and listing documents in the prompt does not process them.

q: A startup wants its web service to read and edit files and run shell commands on a repository, using the same tools and permission system as Claude Code, without writing the tool implementations. What is the MOST direct route?
opts: Use the Message Batches API with all of the file contents inlined
Embed the Claude Agent SDK in the service and configure its allowed tools
Call the Messages API and implement bash and file editing yourself from scratch
Run the interactive CLI in a terminal session and screen-scrape its output
why: The Agent SDK packages the Claude Code agent loop, built-in tools and permissions as a library for Python and TypeScript. Re-implementing tools on the raw API is possible but far more work, the Batches API does not run tools, and scraping an interactive terminal is fragile.

q: Which TWO conditions favor building a workflow with fixed code paths instead of an autonomous agent? (Choose two.)
opts: Each next action depends on what earlier tool results turn out to contain
The sequence of steps is known ahead of time and must be repeatable and testable
Predictable latency and cost matter more than flexibility
The task is open-ended and the number of steps cannot be estimated
why: Workflows suit known steps, repeatability, easy testing and predictable cost and latency. Agents suit tasks where the next action depends on observations and the number of steps cannot be known, which are the other two conditions.

q: Which TWO are genuine benefits of delegating a subtask to a subagent? (Choose two.)
opts: It guarantees a correct result because a second agent has checked it
Independent subtasks can run in parallel and finish in the time of the slowest
It automatically sees everything the parent has already said to the user
Its intermediate tool calls and file reads stay out of the parent's context window
why: Subagents isolate context, since only their final message returns, and they allow parallel work. They do not inherit the parent's conversation and delegation does not by itself make results correct.

q: A lead agent is writing the task prompt for a bug-fixing subagent. Which THREE items belong in that prompt? (Choose three.)
opts: Decisions already made with the user, such as "do not change the public API"
The file paths and function names involved
The exact error message and how to reproduce it
A one-line instruction to "fix the bug we talked about"
A note that the subagent can read the parent's earlier tool results
why: A subagent starts with a fresh context, so the prompt must carry the locations, the error and the constraints. It cannot read the parent's earlier tool results, and a vague pointer to a prior conversation tells it nothing.

q: An agent run needs protection against runaway loops and unexpected cost. Which TWO controls are enforced by the harness regardless of what the model decides? (Choose two.)
opts: A maximum number of tool-using turns
A maximum spend budget for the run
A system prompt line asking the model to finish quickly
A friendly reminder in CLAUDE.md to avoid long tasks
why: Turn and budget limits stop the loop in code and return a result with an error subtype. Prompt and CLAUDE.md wording only influences the model.

q: Which TWO mechanisms keep an agent from using a dangerous tool even if the model decides to try? (Choose two.)
opts: A PreToolUse hook that denies matching calls
A disallowed-tools entry that blocks the tool outright
A CLAUDE.md section titled "Safety rules"
A paragraph in the system prompt explaining why the tool is dangerous
why: Hooks and deny lists are applied by the harness before the tool runs, so they hold regardless of the model's choice. Prompt and CLAUDE.md text is context the model weighs, not an enforced rule.

q: For which TWO needs is Claude Managed Agents a GOOD fit? (Choose two.)
opts: Long-running tasks that run for minutes or hours and may be checked on later
A requirement for zero data retention across all requests
Avoiding building your own agent loop, sandbox and tool execution layer
A sub-second single-turn autocomplete feature
why: Managed Agents targets long-running asynchronous work and removes the need to build the harness and sandbox. Its sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so it is not currently eligible for zero data retention, and a one-turn low-latency feature is better served by the Messages API.

q: An Agent SDK run stops with the error_max_turns subtype. Which TWO responses are appropriate? (Choose two.)
opts: Print the result text field, which always holds the finished reply
Read the session ID from the result and resume the session with a higher limit
Assume the task completed and mark the job successful
Log the usage and cost fields, which are present on every result subtype
why: Limit stops are not successes: capture the session ID to resume, and record the cost and usage that every subtype carries. The result text exists only for the success subtype.

q: A subagent automatically inherits the full conversation history of the agent that started it.
opts: True
False
why: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context. The only content passed from parent to subagent is the task prompt, so the parent must include the files, errors and decisions the subagent needs.

q: In prompt chaining, a programmatic check can sit between steps to catch problems before the next model call.
opts: True
False
why: Gates between steps are a defining feature: code validates the intermediate output and stops or corrects the flow early, which is why chains are easy to test.

q: When Claude returns a tool_use block, the model itself has already executed the client tool.
opts: True
False
why: For client tools the model only emits a structured request. Your application runs the operation and returns the outcome in a tool_result. Only server tools such as web search are executed by Anthropic.

q: Agent SDK hooks run in your application process, so a hook's own code does not consume tokens from the model's context window.
opts: True
False
why: Hooks are callbacks executed by the harness, outside the model's context. They can block, modify or log tool calls without costing context tokens, unless they inject context deliberately.

q: The bypassPermissions mode is appropriate for isolated environments such as containers and CI, where the agent's actions cannot affect systems you care about.
opts: True
False
why: It runs allowed tools without prompting, so reserve it for sandboxed settings. Interactive applications should use the default mode with an approval callback.

q: Using an agentic framework removes the need to understand the tool_use and tool_result contract.
opts: True
False
why: Frameworks wrap the loop but the contract underneath is unchanged. Debugging, cost control and error handling still depend on knowing what is exchanged with the API.

q: With a self-hosted sandbox in Managed Agents, tool inputs and outputs never reach Anthropic.
opts: True
False
why: Orchestration of the loop stays on Anthropic's side, so tool inputs and results flow to its control plane for the model to read. What stays in your environment is execution, files and network egress.

q: An evaluator-optimizer loop should have a cap on the number of revision rounds.
opts: True
False
why: Without a cap a generator and critic can keep revising indefinitely, spending tokens without convergence. A cap guarantees termination.

q: In the Agent SDK, the maximum turns option counts tool-use turns, not the final text-only response.
opts: True
False
why: The limit applies to tool-using round trips. If it is reached before the model finishes, the result carries the error_max_turns subtype.

q: For best reliability, every new Claude application should start as a fully autonomous multi-agent system and be simplified later.
opts: True
False
why: The guidance is the opposite: start with the simplest design that meets the requirement, such as a single call or a workflow, and add autonomy only when the problem demands it.

q: When a PreToolUse hook denies a tool call, the model receives a rejection message and may try a different approach.
opts: True
False
why: A denied call does not execute. The rejection is returned to the model as the tool result, so it can change course or explain that it could not proceed.

q: A product has a live chat widget that must start showing words within a couple of seconds, plus a nightly job that tags the day's chat transcripts for analytics, which nobody reads until morning. Which architecture BEST matches the two requirements?
opts: Send both workloads through synchronous Messages API calls, because one integration is simpler to run
Stream chat replies through the Messages API and submit the nightly tagging as a Message Batches job
Send both workloads through the Message Batches API, because batch pricing is lower for everything
Send chat through the Message Batches API and poll every second so that replies feel immediate
why: Match each workload to its latency need. Chat has a person waiting, so it needs a synchronous, streamed call. The tagging job is latency-tolerant and benefits from the lower batch price and higher throughput. Batching the chat cannot meet a seconds-level target, and running the overnight job synchronously pays full price for no benefit.

q: A public-sector customer requires that model inference for its requests run only on US infrastructure. The app calls the direct Claude API with a Claude 4.6-generation or later model. What is the BEST way to meet the requirement?
opts: Write a sentence in the system prompt asking Claude to use only servers located in the US
Set inference_geo to us on requests or as the workspace default, and check the usage field
Send an anthropic-version header value that names a particular US region for the request
Set the same parameter while calling an older model, since the setting applies retroactively
why: Data residency for inference is controlled by the inference_geo setting, either per request or as a workspace default, and the response usage reports where inference ran. Prompt text cannot move computation, the parameter is rejected with a 400 on models before the 4.6 generation, and the version header selects an API contract rather than a region.

q: A stakeholder asks for "an assistant that is accurate and fast" and gives no further detail. What should the developer do FIRST?
opts: Set a small max_tokens value so that replies are short, and so fast and accurate as well
Select the most capable model that is available and settle the other details afterwards
Build the user interface first, so that the stakeholder can react to something concrete
Turn it into measurable targets: accuracy on a labeled set, p95 latency, cost per request
why: Requirements work comes before design: vague quality words become testable acceptance criteria that drive model choice, caching, evals and architecture. Choosing the strongest model or building a UI first guesses at the target, and a small output cap trades completeness for speed and does not improve accuracy.

q: A company has standardized on AWS: workloads authenticate with IAM roles, spend is consolidated on the AWS bill, and security forbids storing third-party API keys. Which approach to reach Claude BEST fits?
opts: Use an AWS-integrated offering such as Claude in Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS
Host the Claude model weights on company-owned GPU instances inside the AWS account
Call the direct Claude API from EC2 with an API key kept in an environment variable
Use the Message Batches API, which accepts IAM roles directly from the calling service
why: Cloud-platform access lets Claude requests use the provider's IAM and billing, which matches the stated infrastructure requirements. A direct-API key contradicts the policy, Anthropic does not distribute Claude weights for self-hosting, and the batch endpoint authenticates the same way as the rest of the direct API.

q: At peak, a support app sends about 800 requests per minute, each with roughly 4,000 input tokens (3,500 of them an identical instruction and policy block, longer than the model's minimum cacheable length) and about 300 output tokens. The organization's limits for the model are 1,000 requests, 2,000,000 input tokens and 400,000 output tokens per minute, and calls return 429 at peak. Which action BEST addresses the cause?
opts: Merge calls together to push the request count below the requests-per-minute limit
Lower max_tokens so that the output-token limit is never reached during the peak period
Retry each failed call immediately in a tight loop until one of them finally succeeds
Cache the identical 3,500-token prefix so cache reads stop counting toward the input limit
why: Input tokens are 800 x 4,000 = 3.2 million per minute, above the 2 million limit, while requests (800) and output tokens (about 240,000) are within their limits. For most models cache reads do not count toward the input limit, so caching the shared prefix cuts counted input to roughly 0.4 million. max_tokens does not factor into output-limit accounting, the request count is already fine, and tight retries only add load.

q: A health-tech company has a zero data retention arrangement and must answer questions about patient PDFs. Which design keeps the PDF handling inside that arrangement?
opts: Submit every one of the PDFs as requests inside a single Message Batches job
Send each PDF inline as a base64 document block in a standard Messages API call
Create a Managed Agents session and attach all of the PDFs to it as files
Upload each PDF once through the Files API and reference the returned file ID
why: Standard Messages API calls with inline PDF content are eligible for zero data retention. The Files API keeps files until deleted or expired, batches keep requests and results for up to 29 days, and Managed Agents sessions are stateful and stored, so each of those falls outside the arrangement for that data.

q: An email says the model your production application calls will be retired in 70 days, and names a replacement. What is the BEST plan?
opts: Run evals on the replacement, fix any differences, then roll out gradually before the date
Wait until the retirement date and switch only if requests begin to fail in production
Pin the model in a new configuration file, since pinned models are never retired
Ask support to keep the model available indefinitely and take no action in the meantime
why: Deprecation is a planned lifecycle event with notice, so use the window to test the replacement against your own tasks and migrate in stages. Waiting risks an outage, every model ID has its own retirement schedule so pinning does not prevent it, and an open-ended extension cannot be assumed.

q: A team edits prompts several times a week and wants confidence that a change has not hurt quality before it reaches users. Which life-cycle practice fits BEST?
opts: Deploy to all users and watch the support queue for complaints about the new behavior
Read three sample outputs by hand, and deploy the change if they look fine to you
Skip testing, because prompts are only text and cannot break anything in production
Run an eval suite in CI on each prompt or model change and gate merges on the scores
why: Treat a prompt change as a release: automated evals on a representative set catch regressions before deployment and make quality measurable. Spot checks miss edge cases, learning from complaints puts users in the test group, and prompts can break behavior as surely as code.

q: Three months after launch, extraction quality has quietly dropped for a new invoice layout. Nothing in the code changed and no alert fired. Which operational practice would have surfaced this earliest?
opts: A quarterly review of the architecture diagram with the whole engineering team present
Turning off request logging altogether in order to reduce the cost of storage
Writing a larger number of unit tests for the HTTP client that calls the model API
Production monitoring that scores sampled live outputs and alerts on quality drops
why: Quality in an LLM app can drift because the inputs change even when code does not. Sampling and scoring live traffic, with versions recorded, detects this early and shows where it started. Diagram reviews and HTTP unit tests do not observe model output, and removing logs removes the evidence.

q: A bad prompt edit caused a spike of malformed outputs. Rolling back took hours because prompts are edited directly in a dashboard with no history. What change BEST prevents a repeat?
opts: Duplicate the dashboard prompt into a second dashboard so there is always a backup
Keep prompts in version control, review changes, and log the prompt version per response
Make the dashboard editor read-only for everyone on the team, permanently from now on
Ask the model to remember the previous version of the prompt text between calls
why: Versioned prompts make a change reviewable, attributable and reversible, and the logged version lets you tie a regression to an edit. A permanent lock stops improvement, a second dashboard copy has no history either, and the model has no memory of earlier prompt versions between calls.

q: A team will move 2 million users from one Claude model to a newer one. Which rollout approach BEST limits risk?
opts: Let each user pick the model in their settings and collect no metrics on the results
Run the new model only in staging and then switch production without any further checks
Switch every user at once at midnight, since the vendor has already tested the new model
Send a small share of traffic to the new model behind a flag, compare metrics, then ramp up
why: A canary or gradual rollout exposes few users to a regression and gives real data to compare, while the flag makes rollback immediate. Switching everyone at once or relying on staging alone skips production evidence, and user choice without metrics gives no basis for a decision.

q: A support chatbot built on the Messages API answers each question correctly in isolation but forgets everything the user said earlier. Each request currently contains only the newest user message. What is the right fix?
opts: Resend the accumulated user and assistant turns with every request
Move the user's earlier questions into the top-level system field once
Pass the previous response ID so the server can restore the conversation
Raise max_tokens so that the model has more room available to remember things
why: The Messages API is stateless: the server keeps no memory between calls, so the application must resend the prior turns each time (and decide how to trim or summarise them as they grow). There is no response-ID restore mechanism, an output cap does not store anything, and the system field is for standing instructions, not a transcript.

q: A pipeline calls json.loads on Claude's reply and fails intermittently on very long invoices; the failing replies end in the middle of a string. What is the MOST likely cause and best fix?
opts: The stop reason is max_tokens: check it before parsing, then raise the limit or stream
The reply needs an assistant prefill containing an opening brace before it can complete
The model is non-deterministic, so retry the identical request until the JSON happens to parse
The prompt lacks the words "valid JSON only", so add them to the end of the prompt in capitals
why: A reply that stops mid-string was cut off at the output cap. Branching on stop_reason before parsing identifies it, and a larger limit (with streaming for big outputs) fixes it. Identical retries will truncate at the same point, emphasis in the prompt does not change the cap, and prefill is not supported on current models.

q: Users of a writing assistant complain that nothing appears for about 20 seconds while long drafts are generated. Without changing the model, which change BEST improves responsiveness?
opts: Submit each request as a batch job and poll for the finished result every few seconds
Stream the response over server-sent events and render the text deltas as they arrive
Cut max_tokens to 200 so that every draft is always short enough to return quickly
Send every request twice in parallel and show the draft from whichever returns first
why: Streaming starts delivering tokens immediately, so the first words appear quickly even though total generation time is unchanged. Batches are slower by design, a tiny output cap breaks the product, and duplicate requests double cost without addressing time to first token.

q: A developer streams a response that includes a tool call, runs json.loads on each partial_json fragment as it arrives, and gets parse errors. What should the code do instead?
opts: Accumulate the fragments and parse the JSON once the content block has stopped
Disable streaming for every single request that happens to define any tools at all
Wrap each parse in a catch block and keep going with the partial, broken data
Ask the model to emit larger fragments by raising the max_tokens value on the request
why: Tool inputs stream as partial JSON strings that are only valid once complete, so accumulate them and parse after the content_block_stop event (the SDK helpers do this for you). Fragment size is not configurable through max_tokens, disabling streaming throws away its benefit, and continuing with broken data corrupts the call.

q: After upgrading to a newer model, requests that end with a prefilled assistant message containing an opening brace now fail with a 400 error. Which fix is BEST?
opts: Add a beta header to the request that is supposed to re-enable assistant prefill
Retry the same request several times with exponential backoff between the attempts
Use structured outputs for guaranteed JSON, or state the format in the system prompt
Downgrade the SDK package to an earlier release that still sends prefill requests
why: Assistant prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, so the request is invalid and will not succeed by retrying. Structured outputs give schema-valid JSON by constrained decoding, and instructions in the system prompt are the lighter alternative. Beta headers and SDK versions do not change what the model accepts.

q: An extraction service needs JSON with exact field names and types. It currently asks for JSON in the prompt and occasionally receives malformed output that must be retried. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Ask for XML output instead of JSON, because XML is considered easier to repair by hand
Pass a JSON Schema via structured outputs and keep validating business rules in code
Strip markdown fences and trailing commas from the reply text with regular expressions
Add five more worked examples to the prompt and keep the existing retry loop in place
why: Structured outputs constrain decoding to the schema so the text parses and has the required fields, which removes most retries. Schema validity still does not guarantee that values are right, so keep semantic validation. Examples and regex repair reduce, but do not eliminate, malformed output, and switching formats just moves the problem.

q: A request using structured outputs returns HTTP 200, but the text does not match the schema. Which explanation and handling are MOST appropriate?
opts: It is probably a refusal or truncation: branch on stop_reason before parsing and handle both
The schema compiler rejected the schema, so a 400 error should have come back instead
Structured outputs failed silently, so repeat the identical request until it finally works
Long prompts switch off schema enforcement, so shorten the prompt until the output parses
why: Schema compliance is guaranteed except when the reply is a refusal (a normal 200 response whose message takes precedence) or when it is truncated by the output cap. Checking the stop reason first tells you which. Schema problems at request time return a 400, and prompt length does not switch enforcement off.

q: A mobile app sends the same twelve high-resolution photos, base64-encoded, on every turn of a long conversation. Requests are slow and approach the payload limit. What is the BEST change?
opts: Drop all earlier photos from the history after the first turn, without telling the user
Re-encode the photos at the lowest JPEG quality, regardless of whether text stays legible
Upload each photo once with the Files API and reference it by file ID in image blocks
Convert every one of the photos into a PDF document before sending it each turn
why: Each turn resends the full history, so inline base64 images inflate every request. File IDs keep payloads small however many images accumulate. Converting to PDF does not shrink the data, silently removing images loses context the user expects the model to have, and aggressive compression can make text unreadable.

q: Users upload .docx and .xlsx files, and a developer's attempts to send them as document blocks fail. What is the BEST approach?
opts: Set the media type to application/pdf and send the original file bytes unchanged
Send each one of the Word and Excel files as an image block instead
Convert them to plain text or PDF first, then send the converted content
Rename the uploaded files so that each one ends with a .pdf extension
why: Document blocks accept PDFs and plain text. Office formats must be converted to text (or to PDF when layout and embedded images matter) before sending. Renaming or relabelling bytes does not change their format, and an image block expects an actual image.

q: A multi-tenant SaaS stores customer uploads with the Files API. A developer proposes letting the browser submit a file ID that the backend passes straight into the message request. What is the main problem?
opts: Files are workspace-wide, so a user-supplied ID could expose another customer's file
The Files API cannot be combined with the Messages API for any kind of content at all
File IDs have to be sent in a separate request header rather than inside content blocks
File IDs expire after a single request and can never be reused in later requests
why: Uploaded files are scoped to the workspace, not to an end user, so any ID that resolves in the workspace can be read by the app's key. Keep the user-to-file mapping on the server, never trust IDs from clients, and consider a separate workspace per tenant. File IDs persist until deleted or expired, and they are referenced inside content blocks.

q: A developer matched Message Batches results to inputs by line position in the results file, and some customers received summaries meant for others. What is the correct practice?
opts: Sort the results file alphabetically by message ID before matching it to the inputs
Match every result back to its input by the custom_id that was set on each request
Submit exactly one request per batch so that the order of results cannot change
Assume the order matches whenever the batch finishes quickly enough to be trusted
why: Batch results can return in any order, so the unique custom_id on each request is the only reliable key. Sorting by message ID or relying on timing does not recover the original order, and one request per batch defeats the purpose of batching.

q: A finished batch reports most requests succeeded, 3 percent errored with invalid_request_error and 1 percent expired. What is the BEST handling?
opts: Retry the invalid requests again unchanged until they eventually start to succeed
Keep the successes, fix the invalid requests, and resubmit those and the expired ones
Resubmit the entire batch from the beginning so that all of the results are consistent
Treat the batch as successful overall and ignore the errored and expired requests
why: Each request is processed independently, and errored, canceled or expired requests are not billed. Repair what was malformed and resubmit only the failed or expired items. Resubmitting everything wastes money, ignoring failures loses data, and an invalid request fails again if sent unchanged.

q: A batch of 50,000 requests ended, and 40 percent errored because of the same mistake in how the request body was built. Nobody noticed until the whole batch had finished. What would have prevented this?
opts: Testing one request of each shape on the Messages API before submitting the batch
Turning on streaming for the batch so that errors show up while it is still running
Waiting for the full 24-hour expiry window to pass before reading any of the results
Splitting the same malformed requests across a larger number of smaller batches
why: Request validation inside a batch happens asynchronously and shows up in the results, so a quick dry run of each request shape on the Messages API catches shape mistakes cheaply. Streaming is not supported for batches, splitting identical bad requests changes nothing, and waiting only delays the discovery.

q: An app sends images by URL to the direct Claude API successfully. After the team moves to Amazon Bedrock, the same requests fail. What is the likely reason and fix?
opts: Bedrock accepts only base64-encoded image sources, so download and encode the images
URL sources need an extra header on Bedrock that carries the host name of the image
Bedrock does not support vision at all, so the images have to be removed from requests
Images must first be uploaded through the Files API before they can be used on Bedrock
why: On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud only base64 sources are currently available for images and documents, whereas the direct API also accepts URLs and file IDs. Vision itself is supported, there is no host header, and the Files API is not the route on those platforms.

q: A tool-using app with thinking enabled starts returning 400 errors on the second turn. The developer rebuilds each assistant message from only its text and tool_use blocks before resending. What is the cause and fix?
opts: The tool_use blocks should have been removed from the history instead of thinking blocks
The thinking blocks were dropped: pass them back unchanged, even ones with empty text
Thinking cannot be combined with tools at all, so thinking has to be turned off
The signature field should be regenerated by the client application before resending it
why: Thinking blocks carry an encrypted signature and, in tool-use conversations, must be returned exactly as received; filtering or editing them in the latest assistant turn is rejected. Removing tool_use blocks would break pairing with results, clients cannot regenerate signatures, and thinking works with tools.

q: A developer enabled prompt caching on a long system prompt but every response shows cache_creation_input_tokens above zero and cache_read_input_tokens at zero. Which cause is MOST likely?
opts: Prompt caching is only available when requests are submitted through the batch endpoint
The prefix changes on each call, such as a timestamp near the start, so nothing matches
Cache reads are reported only in the response headers and never in the usage object
The model ignores cache breakpoints whenever they are placed on a system prompt
why: A cache read requires the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint to be identical to an earlier request (tools, then system, then messages). A varying value early in the prompt makes each call write a new entry. Read counts appear in the usage object, system prompts can be cached, and caching works on the Messages API.

q: Before sending a 300-page contract, a developer wants to know whether it fits the model's context and roughly what it will cost, without generating an answer. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Estimate the count by dividing the size of the file in bytes by a fixed factor of four
Ask Claude in an ordinary chat message how many tokens the attached file is going to use
Send the real request with a large max_tokens value and read the usage object afterwards
Call the token counting endpoint with the same system prompt, tools and document
why: The token counting endpoint accepts the same structure as a message, including system prompt, tools and PDFs, and returns an estimated input count without generating output. Sending the real request spends tokens, a byte-based guess ignores images and tokenizer differences, and the model has no reliable way to count its own input.

q: An intermittent server error needs investigation with Anthropic support. Which piece of information should the application have logged for each failing call?
opts: The complete API key that was used to authenticate the failing call
Only the time of day at which each failing call happened to be made
The request ID returned in the response header and in the error body
A full copy of the whole conversation text written into every single log line
why: Every response carries a unique request ID that support can use to trace the exact call, and error bodies repeat it as request_id. Logging keys is a security risk, timestamps alone are ambiguous, and copying full conversations into logs creates a privacy problem without helping the trace.

q: A non-streaming call that asks for a 100,000-token report makes the SDK raise an error about the expected duration. What is the BEST resolution?
opts: Raise the number of automatic retries that the client performs for each request
Switch to a model that offers a larger context window than the current one
Catch the error and retry the same non-streaming call again until it finally passes
Stream the response, using the final-message helper if events need no handling
why: The SDK refuses non-streaming requests expected to run beyond about ten minutes because idle connections can be dropped. Streaming keeps the connection active, and the final-message helper returns the complete message. Retrying, a bigger context window and extra retries do not change the expected duration.

q: While streaming, a developer needs to know why generation ended so the UI can show a "continue" button after truncation. Where does the stop reason arrive?
opts: Only in a response header that is read after the stream has been closed
In a message_delta event near the end; the first event carries it as null
In the message_start event, which is the very first event of the stream
In every content_block_delta event, as a running value that is updated
why: The initial message object has a null stop_reason, and the real value is delivered in a message_delta event shortly before message_stop. Content block deltas carry content, not the stop reason, and it is part of the event data rather than a header.

q: A nightly job receives a 429 response that includes a retry-after value of 30. What is the BEST way to handle it?
opts: Retry immediately on ten parallel threads to get through before the limit resets
Switch to a second API key from the same organization and continue at full speed
Treat the 429 as a permanent failure and fail the whole nightly job immediately
Wait at least 30 seconds, retry a bounded number of times and lower concurrency
why: The retry-after value says when capacity returns; earlier retries will fail. Waiting, limiting attempts and reducing concurrency respects the limit. Parallel immediate retries make the burst worse, a 429 is transient rather than permanent, and keys in the same organization share its limits.

q: Starting mid-month, every request returns 429 with no retry-after header and a message that the organization crossed its monthly usage threshold. SDK retries keep failing. What is the right conclusion and action?
opts: A monthly spend cap was reached; retries cannot help, so raise the limit or tier
It is an ordinary burst limit, so add jitter to the retry schedule and try again
The API key was revoked, so create a new key and update the deployment
The API is overloaded for everyone, so wait for the incident to clear and retry
why: A tier spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and persists until access resumes at the start of the next month or the limit is raised. Burst limits and overload clear on their own, and a revoked key returns an authentication error rather than a rate-limit error.

q: Monitoring shows bursts of 529 overloaded_error responses across many customers' calls, while your own usage is far below every limit. Which response is MOST appropriate?
opts: Rotate to a new API key in order to get away from the overloaded server
Request a higher rate limit from support, because the current limit is clearly too low
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and keep a degraded or fallback path ready
Fail fast and show an error page, since overload errors cannot be handled in code
why: A 529 reflects temporary capacity pressure across the service, not your quota. Backoff with jitter and a fallback keep the product working. A higher limit or a new key address problems that are not present, and giving up immediately throws away a request that would succeed moments later.

q: A team wrapped every SDK call in its own five-attempt retry loop, not realizing the SDK already retries twice by default. During an incident, traffic to the API triples. What is the BEST correction?
opts: Retry only after a user has clicked a button to confirm that retrying is wanted
Remove every retry from the system so that all errors surface immediately
Treat the layers as one retry budget and set the SDK count or your loop on purpose
Add a third retry layer around the first two for an extra margin of safety
why: Stacked retries multiply attempts (here up to 15 per call), amplifying load exactly when the service is stressed. Decide where retrying lives, cap it and back off. More layers make it worse, no retries throws away transient-failure protection, and a manual button is a poor default.

q: An agent's charge_card tool is wrapped in a timeout-and-retry helper. After a slow response the helper retried, and several customers were charged twice. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Tell the agent in its prompt never to call the charge tool twice for one order
Remove the retry helper from every tool, whatever the tool does or costs
Increase the timeout far enough that retries practically never happen any more
Make the charge idempotent by sending an idempotency key with each logical payment
why: When a call can be repeated, the downstream service must be able to recognise duplicates; an idempotency key makes the repeated request safe. Longer timeouts only reduce the frequency, prompt instructions do not control a helper outside the model, and removing retries trades one failure for another.

q: A script processes 5,000 documents and launches every call at once with a gather over all tasks. The result is a wall of 429 errors. Which change is BEST?
opts: Increase max_tokens so that each call does a larger amount of work than before
Split the 5,000 calls across 5,000 separate processes so that they run independently
Switch the script to plain synchronous calls and remove all of the retry handling
Cap in-flight requests with a semaphore or worker pool sized to the limits, plus backoff
why: Asynchronous code makes unbounded fan-out easy, so bound concurrency and add backoff to stay within limits. If no one is waiting, the batch endpoint is another good option. More processes only fire more requests, and max_tokens does not reduce request volume.

q: An app crashes with an index error when reading content[0].text for certain inputs, although the HTTP status is 200. Which cause and fix are MOST likely?
opts: The server dropped the connection partway through, so retry the same request
The API key lacks permission for this model, so ask an admin to change its role
The reply was a refusal with no content: check stop_reason first and use a fallback
The text block is always the last block in the array, so read the final element
why: A refusal is a normal 200 response whose stop reason is refusal, and the content can be empty. Branch on stop_reason before touching content, and decide on a fallback such as another model. Connection and permission problems would produce errors rather than a 200, and block order is not guaranteed.

q: Which failure should an HTTP client NOT retry automatically?
opts: A 401 authentication error returned after the API key was revoked
A 500 internal error returned by the service on a single request
A 529 overloaded response during a busy period for the whole service
A dropped connection before any response bytes were received at all
why: Authentication failures are not transient; retrying the same revoked key just repeats the failure, so surface the problem and fix the credential. Overload, connection drops and 5xx errors are the classic transient cases suited to retry with backoff.

q: Claude Code produced a 900-line refactor of a payment module, and every existing test passes. What is the BEST step before merging?
opts: Discard the whole change and rewrite the payment module by hand from scratch
Merge it immediately, because every one of the existing tests is already green
Ask the same Claude session that wrote the change to approve its own work
Split it into small commits and have an engineer review the diff before merging
why: Passing tests show only that covered behavior is unchanged. Human code review catches hidden coupling, security problems and logic the tests do not exercise, and smaller commits make that review realistic. Self-approval is not independent, and discarding useful work is wasteful.

q: A team must move a 400,000-line service from one HTTP library to another over six months while still shipping features. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Leave both libraries in the codebase permanently and let each team choose its own
Freeze all feature work and rewrite the entire service in one long-lived branch
Ask Claude to replace every call site in the codebase in a single huge pull request
Add an interface, migrate module by module with tests, then retire the old library
why: A strangler-style incremental migration keeps the system shippable, limits each change so it can be reviewed and rolled back, and ends with the old code removed. A big-bang rewrite is risky and blocks delivery, one enormous pull request cannot be reviewed well, and permanent duplication is technical debt.

q: A team wants Claude Code to review every pull request in CI. Runs must behave the same on every runner, and no secrets may be committed. Which setup is BEST?
opts: Run the CLI with every permission check bypassed, on the shared developer laptops used for CI
Run the CLI non-interactively in bare mode with read-only tools and a key from the secret store
Run the interactive CLI and answer its permission prompts through a screen-scraping script
Commit the API key to a file in a private repository for convenience across all runners
why: Print mode with bare startup skips auto-discovery of local hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md so each runner behaves the same, pre-approved tools avoid prompts, and the key belongs in a secret store. Scraping an interactive session is fragile, committed keys leak, and bypassing permissions on laptops is unsafe.

q: A developer hand-writes an HTTP call to /v1/messages instead of using an SDK and gets a 400 about a missing version. Which request headers does the call need?
opts: Only an authorization header, because the API infers the version on its own
A custom header naming the model, plus the API key header and nothing else
An API key header, the anthropic-version header and a JSON content type
A session cookie copied from a signed-in Claude Console browser tab
why: Direct REST calls need the API key, an anthropic-version value such as 2023-06-01, and content-type application/json; the SDKs add these automatically. The model is specified in the JSON body, and Console cookies are not used for API authentication.

q: A new engineer asks why the team wraps the Anthropic SDK behind its own small interface instead of calling it throughout the codebase. Which reason is MOST sound?
opts: The API rejects calls that arrive from more than one module in the same process
Wrapping the SDK reduces the number of tokens that each individual request uses
One boundary makes retries, logging, model IDs and test fakes easy to change in one place
The SDK is deprecated, so application code is no longer permitted to call it directly
why: A thin adapter centralises cross-cutting concerns and lets tests substitute a fake, which also eases model migrations. The SDK is supported, a wrapper does not change token counts, and the API has no concept of calling modules.

q: A prompt produced neat formatting and knew today's date when tried in the claude.ai chat window, but through the API in the team's app it answers in plain text and gets the date wrong. What explains this?
opts: The API ignores every formatting instruction and always answers in plain text only
claude.ai adds an Anthropic system prompt that the API lacks, so the app must add its own
The current date is stored on the user account and is sent along with API keys
The model behind the API is a weaker version than the one that is used in claude.ai
why: Consumer apps add their own system prompt (current date, formatting habits and more), whereas the API sends only what you provide. To reproduce the behavior, state the date, format and style rules in your own system prompt. The model is not weaker, formatting instructions are honored, and keys do not carry dates.

q: An app summarizes web pages submitted by users. How should the request be structured to keep the page text from being treated as instructions?
opts: Paste the instructions and the page text together in one continuous paragraph
Append the page text to the system prompt so that it carries the highest priority
Ask the authors of the pages not to include anything that looks like a command
Put the instructions in the system prompt and wrap the page in a delimited data block
why: A content boundary separates trusted instructions from untrusted material using structure the model can follow, such as tagged blocks labelled as input data. It is a design aid that works best with least-privilege tools. Putting untrusted text into the system prompt gives it more authority, a blended paragraph hides the boundary, and you cannot control page authors.

q: A tool schema has a free-text type field whose valid values are described only in prose, and about 30 optional parameters. The model often supplies unexpected values. Which redesign helps MOST?
opts: Remove the field descriptions altogether in order to reduce the number of input tokens
Use enums for closed sets, describe each field, and make parameters required where possible
Add a much longer system prompt that repeats all of the valid values for the field
Allow additionalProperties so that the model can add whatever extra fields it likes
why: A schema is both a contract and documentation: enums narrow choices, descriptions explain intent and fewer optional fields reduce ambiguity. A repeated prompt is weaker than a constraint in the schema, extra properties make output less predictable, and removing descriptions removes guidance.

q: After adding dozens of optional fields and several union types to a strict schema, requests fail with a 400 saying the schema is too complex to compile. Which response is BEST?
opts: Retry the same request several times with exponential backoff between the attempts
Remove the schema and parse the prose that comes back with regular expressions
Raise the max_tokens value on the request so the grammar has more room to fit
Simplify it: fewer optional parameters, flatter nesting, strict mode only where needed
why: Complexity limits are about the compiled grammar, so reduce optional parameters and unions, flatten nesting, and reserve strict mode for tools where violations matter. Retrying an unchanged invalid schema fails again, output caps are unrelated, and regex parsing of prose is the brittle approach schemas replace.

q: A developer has corrected Claude Code three times on the same bug in one long session, and answers are getting worse. Which step is BEST?
opts: Switch the project over to a different programming language for the fix
Clear the session and restart with a sharper prompt that includes what was learned
Keep correcting the same mistake, since the model will eventually learn from it
Paste the entire transcript of the session back in again as a new message
why: Repeated failed corrections fill context with dead ends. A clean session with a better prompt almost always beats a long cluttered one. More corrections add to the clutter, pasting the transcript recreates it, and changing languages is unrelated.

q: An engineer wants to understand how a large legacy module works before editing it. Reading it directly would flood the working session with file contents. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Run the research in a separate, unrelated project directory on the same machine
Delegate the research to a subagent that returns a summary, sparing the main context
Read every file in the main session and compact the conversation afterwards
Skip the research entirely and make the edit based only on the file names
why: Subagents explore in their own context window and return only a concise report, which protects the main session. Reading everything into the main context costs space and attention, guessing from names risks errors, and a separate project loses the repository context.

q: A team installed fourteen Claude Code plugins. Sessions feel slower and token usage creeps up, yet most plugins are rarely invoked. What is the MOST appropriate action?
opts: Disable unused plugins, because their skill descriptions occupy context on every turn
Ignore the problem, because plugins that are not being used cannot add any cost
Rename the plugins so that their skill descriptions end up a good deal shorter
Install additional plugins whose job is to compress the output of the other plugins
why: An enabled plugin places the names and descriptions of its skills and agents in context on every turn, and its hooks and servers run alongside sessions, so unused ones carry a cost. Disabling or removing them is the fix. They are not free, and renaming does not remove the overhead.

q: A team lead wants every contributor to a repository to have the same code-review plugin enabled by default. Which install scope is BEST?
opts: Project scope, which records the plugin as enabled in the committed project settings
User scope on the lead's own machine, so it follows the lead into every project
No install scope at all; just email the teammates the manual installation steps
Local scope, so the plugin applies only to the lead and only in this repository
why: Project scope writes the enabled plugin into the shared settings file that is committed, so contributors get the same setup (each still installs it on their own machine). User and local scopes affect only one person, and informal instructions drift.

q: A developer is about to install a plugin from a marketplace that nobody on the team has reviewed. What is the BEST precaution?
opts: Install it straight away and delete it again if anything looks odd afterwards
Install it at user scope, because that scope sandboxes it from the rest of the machine
Trust it, because every plugin marketplace is operated and reviewed by Anthropic itself
Review its hooks, commands and MCP servers first, because it runs with your privileges
why: A plugin can run code, hooks and servers as you, whichever marketplace it comes from, so review the contents before installing. Scope does not sandbox anything, third-party marketplaces exist, and damage from a malicious plugin may happen before you notice anything.

q: An agent fetches web pages with a client tool. Where should the application place the fetched page text when it replies to Claude?
opts: Inside the tool_result block that answers that particular tool call
In the system prompt, so the model fully trusts the fetched content
In an assistant message that the application writes on the model's behalf
As a new user text block placed ahead of the tool result block
why: Untrusted material returned by tools belongs in tool_result content, which keeps it separate from your instructions and keeps the required pairing with the tool_use block. System text is treated as trusted instructions, text before the result breaks the ordering rule, and assistant messages are for the model's own output.

q: A team shares Claude Code settings that select the sonnet alias. After a new Sonnet release, behavior changes for everyone overnight. What is the BEST way to prevent surprise changes?
opts: Switch to the opus alias instead, because that alias never moves to a new version
Disable automatic updates to the Claude Code application for the whole team
Keep the alias and ask everyone on the team to re-check their prompts every week
Pin the full model name in shared settings and migrate deliberately after running evals
why: Aliases point at the recommended newest version and move over time, so shared configurations that want stability should pin an explicit model. Weekly manual checks are unreliable, application updates are not what changed, and every family alias moves.

q: A developer wants sandbox URLs and personal test data available to Claude in one repository without committing them. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Use a local instructions file at the project root and add it to the ignore list
Place them in the organization-managed policy file so they apply to every developer
Paste them into the very first prompt of every session by hand each time
Add them to the shared project CLAUDE.md so that every teammate benefits as well
why: A local instructions file loads alongside the project CLAUDE.md for this repository only, and ignoring it keeps personal data out of source control. The shared file and managed policy expose the data to others, and retyping it every session is tedious and error-prone.

q: An organization requires that no developer ever runs Claude Code with permission checks bypassed, even if individuals set it in their own settings. Where should the rule be placed?
opts: In the project's local settings file kept next to the shared project settings
In every developer's own user settings file under their home directory
In managed settings, which take precedence over every other settings scope
In the shared project CLAUDE.md, written down as a clearly worded policy
why: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order, above the command line, local, project and user settings, so individuals cannot override them. The other locations are overridable or are guidance rather than enforced configuration.

q: A project's CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines and Claude Code seems to ignore some rules. What is the MOST effective improvement?
opts: Trim it to concise, specific instructions and move situational guidance to skills
Add more rules so that each of the rules that are being missed is repeated again
Split it into twenty imported files, because imported files do not load at launch
Add bold and capital-letter emphasis to the important rules so they stand out more
why: Long files consume context and reduce adherence, and contradictions make behavior unpredictable. Keep the file short and specific, and load situational guidance on demand. Imported files are still loaded at launch, so splitting does not help, and adding rules makes it longer.

q: The authors of a plugin depend on another plugin, secrets-vault, with no version constraint. A new release of secrets-vault renamed a tool, and the dependent plugin broke for everyone who updated. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Declare a version range such as ~2.1.0 on the dependency, widening it only after testing
Remove the dependency and ask each user to install that other plugin by hand
Tell all of the users never to update any plugin they have installed, at any time
Copy the dependency's code into the plugin permanently so that it can never change
why: An unconstrained dependency moves to every new release. A tested range keeps users on compatible patches until the author deliberately widens it. Freezing all updates blocks fixes, copying code forks it, and manual installation reintroduces drift.

q: An app has separate development, staging and production deployments. An engineer hard-codes one API key in a config file in the repository. What is the BEST correction?
opts: Encode the key in base64 inside the config file so that it is no longer readable
Keep the key in the repository but make the repository private to the team
Share the production key with every environment so that all of them stay identical
Read keys from the environment or a secret manager, with a workspace per environment
why: Keys belong outside source control, supplied per environment, with workspaces separating environments and their limits and spend. A private repository still leaks to everyone with access and to history, a shared production key widens the blast radius, and base64 is not encryption.

q: Which TWO of the following are non-functional requirements for a Claude-powered support assistant? (Choose two.)
opts: The assistant must summarize each ticket in three sentences
The assistant must call the refund tool for eligible orders
Model inference for EU customers must stay in an approved geography
Ninety-five percent of replies must begin streaming within three seconds
why: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, throughput, availability, cost and data residency. Summarizing tickets and calling a refund tool describe what the system does, so they are functional.

q: Which TWO workloads are good candidates for the Message Batches API? (Choose two.)
opts: Answering a customer typing in a live chat window
Completing the next line of code as a developer types
Re-tagging an archive of 200,000 documents with a new taxonomy by next week
Scoring a 20,000-prompt evaluation set overnight
