why: Batches are cheaper and high-throughput but promise results only within 24 hours, so they fit latency-tolerant bulk work. Live chat and as-you-type completion have a person waiting and need synchronous calls.

q: A team wants safe, repeatable changes to prompts and model versions. Which TWO practices support that? (Choose two.)
opts: Store prompts in version control and release them through review
Switch the production model alias whenever a new release appears
Edit the live prompt directly during an incident without recording the change
Run an evaluation suite in CI and gate merges on its scores
why: Versioned, reviewed prompts and automated evals make changes traceable, testable and reversible. Untracked live edits and automatic alias changes remove that safety and make regressions hard to trace.

q: A client consumes a streamed Messages API response. Which THREE behaviors make it robust? (Choose three.)
opts: Ignore ping events and keep reading
Parse every partial JSON fragment of a tool call as soon as it arrives
Read the final stop reason from the first event in the stream
Handle an error event that arrives after the HTTP 200
Skip event types it does not recognise instead of crashing
why: Streams can contain ping events, mid-stream error events, and new event types added over time, so a robust client tolerates all three. The stop reason is null at the start and arrives in a later message_delta, and partial JSON is valid only after the block finishes.

q: A reply arrives with stop_reason tool_use. Which TWO things must the next request contain? (Choose two.)
opts: The tool_result blocks placed before any other content in the user message
A new anthropic-version value reserved for tool turns
An assistant message restating the tool output in the model's voice
A tool_result for every tool_use ID in the previous reply
why: Each tool_use needs a matching result in a user message that follows the assistant turn, with the results first. Results are never sent as assistant text, and the version header does not change per turn.

q: Which THREE are valid ways to supply an image to the Messages API on the direct Claude API? (Choose three.)
opts: A path to a file on the application server
Raw bytes placed inside a text block
A file ID from the Files API
A URL that points to the image
A base64-encoded string with a media type
why: Image blocks accept base64, URL and file sources. The API cannot read a path on your server, and image bytes in a text block are not interpreted as an image.

q: Which TWO statements about the Message Batches API are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Results are guaranteed within five minutes
Results can come back in a different order from the requests
It is charged at half the standard price
It supports streaming so results arrive token by token
why: Batch usage costs 50 percent of standard prices and results are matched by custom_id because order is not guaranteed. Streaming is not supported, and processing can take up to 24 hours, although most batches finish within an hour.

q: Which TWO errors are normally worth retrying with exponential backoff? (Choose two.)
opts: A 429 response that includes a retry-after header
A 401 authentication_error for a revoked key
A 400 invalid_request_error caused by an unsupported parameter
A 529 overloaded_error response
why: Overload and burst rate limits are transient and clear with time. A malformed request or a bad credential stays wrong until you change it, so retrying only adds noise.

q: A bulk job keeps hitting 429 errors. Which THREE changes help? (Choose three.)
opts: Raise max_tokens so each call does more
Bound the number of in-flight requests
Retry every failed call immediately with no delay
Honor the retry-after value before retrying
Ramp traffic up gradually instead of starting at full volume
why: Limiting concurrency, waiting as instructed and avoiding sudden jumps respect token-bucket and acceleration limits. Instant retries worsen the burst, and max_tokens does not affect request counts.

q: A team uses Claude Code to help with a large refactoring. Which TWO practices reduce risk? (Choose two.)
opts: Keep refactoring commits separate from feature changes
Make small steps and keep the test suite green after each one
Skip human review because the changes were written by a model
Land the whole change as a single enormous pull request
why: Small, tested, single-purpose steps are easier to review, bisect and revert. One giant change and skipped review remove those safeguards.

q: Why do model-generated changes still need human code review even when all tests pass? (Choose two.)
opts: Plausible but wrong logic and design problems can pass tests
Tests do not cover every behavior or security property
Model-generated code cannot be syntactically valid
The hosting platform refuses to merge any unreviewed pull request
why: Green tests only prove the covered behavior, so review is where hidden coupling, security flaws and subtly wrong logic are caught. Generated code is usually valid syntax, and merge rules are a team policy rather than a platform fact.

q: Which TWO are good practices when designing JSON Schemas for tool inputs and structured outputs? (Choose two.)
opts: Make most parameters optional so the model has flexibility
Allow arbitrary extra properties to avoid validation failures
Write clear descriptions for fields whose meaning is not obvious
Use enums for fields with a closed set of valid values
why: Enums constrain choices and descriptions tell the model what each field means. Many optional parameters and open-ended extra properties increase ambiguity and compile complexity.

q: Which THREE habits keep an interactive Claude Code session effective? (Choose three.)
opts: Delegating broad codebase research to a subagent
Restarting with a sharper prompt after repeated failed corrections
Keeping one session open forever so it learns everything
Pasting the full output of every command into the chat
Clearing the session between unrelated tasks
why: Context is the scarce resource: reset it between tasks, avoid carrying dead ends, and keep exploration in separate contexts. A permanent session and pasting everything fill the window with irrelevant material.

q: Which TWO statements about CLAUDE.md files are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Block-level HTML comments in them are sent to the model with the rest of the text
They are loaded as context, not as enforced configuration
A project file always replaces the user-level file
Files found at different levels are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other
why: All discovered files are combined, with instructions closer to the working directory read last, and Claude treats them as guidance, so use hooks or permission rules to enforce. HTML block comments are stripped before injection, and project files do not replace user files.

q: A team will migrate from one Claude model to a newer one. Which TWO practices support a safe migration? (Choose two.)
opts: Run your own eval suite on the candidate and compare results to the current model
Pin the exact model ID in production while the candidate is evaluated
Wait for the retirement date, then pick a replacement
Change the alias in production first and watch what breaks
why: Pinning keeps production stable while you measure the candidate on your own tasks. Switching blindly or waiting until retirement removes the safety margin that the notice period provides.

q: The Messages API keeps the conversation on the server between requests, so a client only needs to send the newest user message.
opts: True
False
why: The API is stateless. The application must send the full history it wants the model to see with every request.

q: A 429 caused by reaching a monthly spend cap will not be fixed by SDK automatic retries.
opts: True
False
why: That variant has no retry-after header and persists until the limit is raised or the next month begins. Retrying only repeats the failure.

q: A refusal from the model's safety classifiers is returned as an HTTP 4xx error, so exception handling is enough to catch it.
opts: True
False
why: A refusal is a normal 200 response with stop_reason refusal. Code must check the stop reason, because no exception is raised.

q: An error can arrive inside a streamed response even though the HTTP status was already 200.
opts: True
False
why: Once streaming starts, the status line has been sent. Failures such as overloaded_error are delivered as error events in the stream, so streaming code needs its own handling.

q: Message Batches API requests cost half of standard prices, and results are matched to requests by custom_id because order is not guaranteed.
opts: True
False
why: Both statements are correct. Batch usage is charged at 50 percent of standard prices, and results can return in any order.

q: Files you upload through the Files API can be downloaded again later with the download endpoint.
opts: True
False
why: Only files created by skills or the code execution tool are downloadable. Downloading a file you uploaded returns an error, so keep your own copy.

q: On the direct Claude API, an image block can use a base64 source, a URL source or a file ID source.
opts: True
False
why: All three source types are supported. Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud currently accept only base64.

q: Structured outputs guarantee that every value in the returned JSON is factually correct.
opts: True
False
why: They guarantee the shape (valid JSON that matches the schema), not the truth of the values. Semantic validation and verification are still your job.

q: Assistant prefill remains supported on Claude 4.6 and later models.
opts: True
False
why: A prefilled final assistant message is rejected with a 400 error on those models. Use structured outputs or system prompt instructions instead.

q: Server-sent events used for Claude streaming allow the browser and server to exchange messages in both directions over the same connection.
opts: True
False
why: SSE is one-way, server to client. A WebSocket is the bidirectional alternative, and the Claude API streams responses with SSE.

q: The max_tokens parameter is a target length that the model tries to reach.
opts: True
False
why: It is only a ceiling. The model usually stops sooner, and if it reaches the cap the reply is cut off with stop_reason max_tokens.

q: The official SDKs retry transient failures such as connection errors, 429 and 5xx responses twice by default.
opts: True
False
why: Automatic retries with short exponential backoff are on by default and can be changed with max_retries per client or per request.

q: Using asynchronous code makes a single model request return faster.
opts: True
False
why: Async lets one process overlap many requests, which raises throughput. Each individual call still takes as long as the model needs.

q: Prompts, tool schemas and configuration files belong in version control alongside the source code.
opts: True
False
why: They determine behavior as much as code does, so changes should be reviewed, traceable and reversible.

q: A feature flag can switch traffic back to the previous prompt without redeploying the application.
opts: True
False
why: Flags are runtime switches, which is what makes gradual rollout and instant rollback possible.

q: A dateless model ID from the Claude 4.6 generation onward, such as claude-sonnet-4-6, is a fixed snapshot rather than a pointer that quietly moves to newer releases.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic does not change the weights behind an existing model ID; updated versions ship under new IDs. Convenience aliases that move exist for earlier models and in tools such as Claude Code.

q: After a model's retirement date, requests that name it fail.
opts: True
False
why: Retired models are no longer available. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice for public models, which is the window to migrate.

q: Updates to the system prompt used in claude.ai also change how the Claude API behaves.
opts: True
False
why: The consumer apps' system prompt is separate. Those updates do not apply to the API, which uses only the instructions you send.

q: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files from the working directory and from every directory above it at launch, and combines them.
opts: True
False
why: Files up the directory tree are concatenated, ordered from the root down to the working directory. Subdirectory files load later, on demand.

q: A plugin dependency declared without a version constraint follows each new release its marketplace publishes.
opts: True
False
why: That is why authors add a tested range such as ~2.1.0 when a new release could break the dependent plugin.

q: Enabling a plugin at project scope automatically installs it on every teammate's machine with no further action.
opts: True
False
why: The committed settings record that the plugin should be enabled, but each collaborator still installs it on their own machine.

q: A requirement that 95 percent of replies start within three seconds is a functional requirement.
opts: True
False
why: Latency targets describe how well the system performs, so they are non-functional requirements. Functional requirements describe what the system does.

q: Usage of the Message Batches API reduces the rate limits available to the synchronous Messages API.
opts: True
False
why: Batches have their own limits, and using them does not affect Messages API rate limits.

q: The token counting endpoint returns an exact count that will always equal the billed input tokens.
opts: True
False
why: The count is an estimate and can differ by a small amount from actual usage, so treat it as a planning tool and rely on the usage object for billing.

q: Committing an API key to a private repository is an acceptable way to share it with a team.
opts: True
False
why: Keys in source control spread to everyone with access and live on in history. Use a secret manager or environment variables, with separate workspaces per environment.

q: A support assistant must answer questions about a 40,000-row order database that changes every minute. The team pastes an export into the system prompt; it barely fits the context window and is minutes out of date. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Raise max_tokens so that the model can hold the entire export in its working memory
Upload a fresh export through the Files API every minute and reference the newest file ID
Give the model a read-only lookup tool that queries the live database for the orders it needs
Send the export through the Message Batches API so that it is processed with each question
why: For large, fast-changing data, let the model fetch only what it needs on demand through a tool: the answer is current, the prompt stays small, and access can be limited to read-only queries. A minute-by-minute upload still sends stale or oversized data into the context, max_tokens limits output rather than memory, and the batch endpoint is asynchronous and unsuited to live questions.

q: A developer installs a plugin at user scope from the Claude Code terminal. Where will it also be available on the same computer without another installation?
opts: In every cloud session run from a browser, because plugins follow the user account
In any teammate's terminal, because user scope shares plugins across the organization
Only in the terminal session where the command was run, until it is restarted
In the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension, but not in cloud sessions
why: The local surfaces read the same settings files, so a user-scope plugin is shared among the terminal, the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension on that machine. A cloud session does not load the plugins in your local settings, user scope applies to one person rather than a team, and the install persists beyond a single terminal session.

q: Because prompts are plain text, tuning a Claude application can safely be treated as a one-time design phase finished before the first release.
opts: True
False
why: Model behavior, inputs and models themselves change, so prompts need measured, repeated iteration: evals on each change, monitoring after release, and migrations when models are deprecated.

q: A repository has test files named *.test.ts spread across forty folders. The team wants Claude Code to follow specific testing conventions whenever it works with those files, without loading them for unrelated work. What is the BEST setup?
opts: A custom slash command that developers must remember to run before any test-related task
A rule file in .claude/rules with a paths pattern of **/*.test.ts, so it loads only when a matching file is used
A paragraph in the root CLAUDE.md, which loads at the start of every session whatever the task, and costs context each time
A copy of the testing conventions in a CLAUDE.md inside each of the forty folders
why: Rules in .claude/rules can carry paths frontmatter with glob patterns; such a rule loads when Claude reads or edits a matching file, so the conventions arrive when relevant and cost nothing otherwise. Forty copies of a CLAUDE.md drift apart and load only per folder, a root paragraph loads in every session, and a manual command depends on people remembering it. If a convention must be enforced rather than followed, use a hook or a permission rule.

q: A CI step runs Claude Code non-interactively to review a diff, and a later script must read a list of issues as a field it can parse and validate. Which invocation is BEST?
opts: claude -p with --output-format stream-json, then wait for the process to exit and parse its first line
claude -p with --output-format json and a --json-schema describing the list, then read the structured_output field
claude -p with default text output, then extract the issues from the prose with regular expressions
An interactive session whose terminal output is recorded and parsed after the review finishes
why: In print mode, --output-format json returns a single JSON object with the result, session ID and usage, and adding --json-schema places a conforming answer in the structured_output field, which a script can parse and validate. Regular expressions over prose are brittle. stream-json emits one event per line with the result at the end, so its first line is not the answer and it suits live progress rather than a single parse, and interactive capture is not a pipeline interface.

q: A developer works in a disposable dev container and is tired of approving every test run and file edit, but the organization still wants a safeguard against actions that stray from the request. Which permission mode fits BEST?
opts: Plan mode, which lets Claude edit files and run commands freely while it drafts a plan
bypassPermissions, which skips the prompts but keeps a safety classifier reviewing each action
acceptEdits, which approves every shell command and network call automatically as well as file edits, whatever the command or its target
Auto mode, where a background classifier reviews actions like shell commands and network requests against the request
why: Auto mode removes routine prompts while a separate classifier checks that actions such as shell commands and network requests align with the request, which fits a team that wants fewer prompts and still a guard. It reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety, and administrators can disable it in managed settings. bypassPermissions skips prompts with no such review and belongs only in isolated environments, acceptEdits approves file edits and common filesystem commands only, and plan mode is read-only exploration without source edits.

q: Midway through a long Claude Code session, a developer wants to try a risky alternative design while keeping the current conversation intact to return to. What is the BEST approach?
opts: Run /branch, or resume with --fork-session, to copy the conversation into a new session and experiment there
Run /compact so the history becomes a summary, then carry on with the new design in the same session
Resume the same session in a second terminal and try the alternative there, which gets its own copy
Run /clear and re-explain the task, relying on the session picker to bring back the old context later
why: /branch (or --continue or --resume combined with --fork-session) copies the transcript into a new session with its own ID; the original stays unchanged on disk and can be resumed later with /resume. Resuming one session in two terminals without forking interleaves both into a single transcript, /compact replaces the history with a summary inside the same session, and /clear starts with an empty context, so the experiment would lose the history it is meant to branch from.

q: A team wants a code-review helper that keeps its own notes about recurring defects in this repository across sessions, with those notes shared with teammates through version control. What is the BEST setup?
opts: A sentence in the root CLAUDE.md asking the main agent to remember recurring defects
A subagent file with memory set to user, so the notes follow each developer across all projects and repositories on their machine
A subagent file with memory set to local, which keeps the notes out of version control
A subagent file in .claude/agents with memory set to project, whose notes go to the committed .claude/agent-memory folder
why: The memory field of a subagent has three scopes: user (a folder under the home directory, shared across all of a developer's projects), project (.claude/agent-memory, meant to be committed and shared with the team) and local (.claude/agent-memory-local, kept out of version control). Only project scope matches notes for this repository shared through git. CLAUDE.md holds instructions you write, not learnings a subagent accumulates.

q: A team is deciding where each kind of guidance should live in Claude Code. Which TWO placements are sound? (Choose two.)
opts: A developer's private sandbox URL is committed in the shared project settings file so it is always available
Instructions that matter only when editing one subfolder are placed at the top of the root CLAUDE.md
The rule that deployments must never touch the production database is enforced by one sentence in CLAUDE.md
A reusable multi-step release procedure goes in a command or skill file in the repository so anyone can invoke it
The build and test commands and the code style conventions go in the committed project CLAUDE.md
why: CLAUDE.md is the place for always-relevant project facts such as commands and conventions, and a command or skill file packages a procedure that is loaded when invoked. A sentence in CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement, so a rule that must hold needs a hook or a permission rule; a private value belongs in CLAUDE.local.md or the local settings file, which stay out of version control; and instructions that matter for one folder belong in a path-scoped rule or a CLAUDE.md in that folder, so they load only when relevant.

q: Running /init in a project that already has a CLAUDE.md replaces the file with a newly generated one.
opts: True
False
why: When a CLAUDE.md already exists, /init suggests improvements instead of overwriting it. On a fresh project it analyzes the codebase and drafts build commands, test instructions and conventions, which you should then review and trim.

q: Claude Code's auto memory notes are stored in the repository and reach teammates through version control.
opts: True
False
why: Auto memory is machine-local: the notes live under the user's own .claude/projects folder (shared by the worktrees of one repository on that machine). The shareable file is the committed CLAUDE.md, which you write yourself.

q: A support bot gives wrong refund-policy answers in production, but the same prompt text run by hand in the Console workbench gives correct ones. Logs show 200 responses with normal stop reasons. What is the BEST first step to find the cause?
opts: Raise max_tokens, since truncated policy text could explain wrong answers even with a normal stop reason
Move to a stronger model tier, since a more capable model answers correctly whatever the request contains and whatever the system prompt says
Capture the exact request body the app sent, replay it unchanged outside the app, and compare it with the hand-built one
Rewrite the system prompt with stricter wording and redeploy it to see whether the answers improve
why: When the same words behave differently in two places, suspect what differs in the request, not the model: an application may send a stale or truncated history, drop the system prompt, omit retrieved policy text or name another model. Replaying the logged request verbatim isolates the origin. If the replay reproduces the bad answer, the fault lies in the request content or the model's behavior; if it answers correctly, the integration layer is assembling or handling something differently. A bigger model, more tokens or new wording treat a symptom without evidence, and the normal stop reason already rules out truncation.

q: A research agent sometimes ends a run by saying it could not find an answer. Aggregate dashboards show normal latency, token use and error rates. Which evidence will MOST directly explain why one specific failed run went wrong?
opts: The text of the agent's closing message on its own, read without any of the steps that produced it
The average number of output tokens per request across the last thirty days of production traffic
The run's trace, showing each model request, tool call, tool input and tool result in order
The daily count of HTTP 200 responses returned by the model endpoint across all of the customers
why: Aggregates hide what happened inside one run. A trace records each step with its inputs, results, timing and status, so you can see a search returning nothing, the same query repeated, a result the model misread, or a handoff missing context, then group runs into failure modes and fix the right layer (tool description, tool output, prompt or context). Averages and success counts cannot localize a failure, and the final text shows only the symptom.

q: A pipeline extracts the invoice total, due date and vendor ID from 5,000 test invoices whose correct values are known. The team needs a fast, repeatable score after every prompt change. Which grading approach is BEST?
opts: Code-based grading that compares each extracted field with its known value after normalizing formats
An LLM judge that reads each extraction and rates how good it looks on a scale of 1 to 5 for every field
Embedding similarity between the extracted text and the full text of the invoice
Human reviewers who read all 5,000 outputs after every prompt change
why: When the right answer has a checkable form, code-based grading is the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method, and exact values call for exact comparison. A rating judge adds cost, variance and fuzziness where none is needed, human review is slow and expensive, and similarity scores cannot tell a correct total from a close-looking wrong one. Keep LLM grading for open-ended qualities such as tone, and use humans to validate graders on samples.

q: A developer edits the system prompt to fix a complaint and checks three conversations by hand before releasing. The next week another behavior is found broken, and nobody can say when it broke. Which practice would have caught this?
opts: Running the full evaluation set on every prompt change and comparing its scores with the stored baseline before merging
Freezing the prompt permanently so that later edits cannot introduce side effects
Asking the model after each edit whether its behavior is still correct for all of the earlier cases, and trusting its own answer
Waiting for support tickets to arrive and treating the ticket volume as the quality measure
why: A prompt change can fix one case and break others. A regression run over a fixed, representative set, wired into the delivery pipeline and gated on scores, catches such side effects before release and shows which edit caused them. The model's own assurance is not a measurement, freezing the prompt blocks improvement, and tickets are a lagging indicator (though real failures should be added to the set as new cases).

q: In a long conversation, cache_read_input_tokens falls to zero on turn 6 although the team believes it only appends messages. They pass the previous response's ID in the diagnostics field, and the reply reports that the system prompt differed from the previous request. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
opts: A timestamp or request ID is inserted into the system prompt; make it constant and put dynamic data after the breakpoint
The five-minute lifetime expired between turns, so the one-hour lifetime has to be enabled from the first turn of the conversation
The conversation grew past the context window, so the oldest messages have to be compacted or dropped
Cache reads are billed separately and are left out of the usage object, so the zero is only a reporting quirk
why: Cache diagnostics compares consecutive requests and reports the first place they diverged. A system-prompt difference means the system parameter changed between turns, typically because a timestamp, request ID or other per-request value was interpolated into it, so the prefix misses every time. Make the system prompt a constant and move dynamic data into a user message after the breakpoint. An expired entry would show no divergence reason with low reads, exceeding the window produces a 400 rather than a cache miss, and cache reads are reported in the usage object.

q: A pipeline's replies suddenly fail schema validation after a deploy that changed only application code. Which TWO checks BEST help decide whether the integration layer or the model's output is at fault? (Choose two.)
opts: Add more instructions about valid JSON to the prompt and redeploy immediately
Inspect the stop_reason and the raw response body of the failing calls before any parsing step runs
Switch the pipeline to a different model tier to see whether the failures disappear
Replay a logged request from before the deploy and one from after it, and compare the two request bodies field by field
Raise the sampling temperature to see whether the failures become random
why: Comparing request bodies from before and after the deploy shows whether the application now sends something different (history, system prompt, max_tokens, schema), and the raw response with its stop_reason shows whether the output was truncated or refused before your code touched it. Together they separate integration faults from model behavior. Changing temperature is not supported on current models and tells you nothing, rewriting the prompt treats a symptom before the cause is known, and switching tiers changes two things at once.

q: Before an LLM-based grader is trusted at scale, its verdicts should be checked against human judgments on a sample.
opts: True
False
why: LLM grading is fast and flexible, but the docs advise testing its reliability first and then scaling: write a detailed rubric, constrain the output (for example correct or incorrect, or a 1 to 5 scale), and compare with human labels on a sample.

q: An evaluation set should contain only typical, well-formed inputs so that its scores stay stable between runs.
opts: True
False
why: Evals should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases such as irrelevant, overlong, ambiguous or harmful inputs. A set without them reports comfortable scores while real traffic fails.

q: A team upgrades a ticket-classification service to Claude Opus 5.5. Every request now fails with a 400 invalid_request_error, and the only change was the model ID. The request still sets temperature to 0 to keep labels stable. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Send the same temperature value inside the output_config object, where newer models expect all of their tuning settings
Replace temperature with top_k set to 1, which forces the single most likely token at every step of the reply
Remove the sampling parameters and get stable labels from clear instructions, varied examples and a constrained output format
Keep the request unchanged and retry each failure, because a 400 on a newly released model is usually transient
why: Claude Opus 5.5, like Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1, rejects any non-default temperature, top_p or top_k with a 400, so the parameters have to go. Consistency now comes from prompt design (clear instructions, varied examples), a constrained output such as structured outputs, and the effort setting. top_k is rejected as well, output_config has no sampling section, and a 400 is a request error that retrying cannot fix. Even temperature 0 never gave fully repeatable text, so tests and pipelines should tolerate variation.

q: A unit test asks Claude to summarize a fixed support ticket and asserts that the reply equals a stored string. It passes on some runs and fails on others although no code changed. What is the BEST way to fix the test?
opts: Call the model twice inside the test and pass only when the two replies come back word for word identical to each other
Re-run the failing test up to ten times and accept the build as soon as one run happens to match the string
Set temperature to 0 so that the stored string is reproduced exactly on every run of the suite
Assert what must hold for any good summary, such as required facts and a length limit, or grade it with a rubric
why: Output from a language model varies from call to call, and even temperature 0 does not make it fully repeatable (current models also reject non-default sampling values). Tests should check properties that must hold, such as facts, format, schema and length, or use a rubric grader. Comparing two replies or retrying until one matches still demands identical wording and only hides the flakiness.

q: A developer runs Claude Sonnet 5.5 at xhigh effort on a hard analysis task and sets max_tokens to 1,500 to keep answers short. Many responses stop with stop_reason max_tokens and contain little or no answer text, even though the thinking display is set to omitted. What explains this, and what is the BEST fix?
opts: Omitted thinking is still generated but billed as input rather than output, so set the display to summarized to release those tokens
Hidden thinking still counts toward max_tokens, so raise the ceiling and control cost with effort and a request for brevity
The xhigh level allocates its own separate token budget, so the truncation must have come from the network layer
Streaming is switched off, so turning streaming on removes the output ceiling for long answers
why: Thinking is billed as output and counts against max_tokens whether or not the text is returned; a display of omitted only hides it. At high effort the reasoning can use up a small ceiling before the visible answer starts. Raise max_tokens (the docs suggest large values at high effort levels), and manage spend through effort and by asking for a concise answer. Display settings change what you see, not what is counted; effort is a soft signal, not a separate allowance; streaming does not change the ceiling.

q: Code written for an earlier model enables reasoning with thinking type enabled and budget_tokens set to 10,000. After the team switches to Claude Opus 5.5, the API returns a 400 error for this field. What is the MOST appropriate change?
opts: Remove the manual budget, let adaptive thinking run, tune its depth with effort, and keep max_tokens as the hard ceiling
Raise budget_tokens to the largest value the model allows, so that the request is no longer treated as invalid by the validation layer of the API
Send thinking type disabled to switch reasoning off, since the budget field is no longer needed at all
Add the extended-thinking beta header to the request so that the budget field is accepted again by the model
why: Manual extended thinking (type enabled with budget_tokens) is not accepted on current models. They use adaptive thinking, which is always on for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, and effort is the control for how much it reasons; max_tokens stays the strict ceiling. A larger budget does not make the type valid, Opus 5.5 rejects thinking disabled with a 400 as well, and the old mode has been removed from these models, so no header brings it back.

q: A team sets effort to low on Claude Opus 5.5 hoping replies never exceed 300 tokens, yet some replies reach 900 tokens. How should the requirement be met?
opts: Move effort to max, because the highest level follows length instructions most strictly of all the levels
Turn on fast mode, which limits how many tokens a reply can contain in return for a premium price
Treat effort as a soft signal: ask for the length needed in the prompt and set max_tokens as the hard ceiling
Lower the temperature, since random sampling is what lets some replies run much longer than others
why: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget: lower levels tend to produce terser output but give no guarantee. For a bound, state the length in the prompt (sentence or paragraph limits work better than word counts) and set max_tokens as the strict ceiling, remembering that a reply cut off at the ceiling may be incomplete. A higher effort level spends more, current models reject non-default temperature, and fast mode speeds up generation without limiting it.

q: A ticket router prompted with instructions only returns labels in inconsistent shapes ('Billing', 'billing issue', 'BILL') and often confuses refunds with billing questions. Which prompting change is MOST likely to fix both problems?
opts: Add three to five varied examples in separate tags, with exact labels, including a refund versus billing edge case
Raise effort to max so the model spends much longer deciding which of the labels fits the ticket
Add one example of a billing ticket so that the model has a format to copy for all of the other categories
Put a line in capital letters at the top of the prompt demanding that the exact label is always used, with no variations at all
why: Multi-shot prompting with several varied, relevant examples teaches format and edge-case handling at once. One example can fix the format but invites the model to copy its quirks and says nothing about the confusing pair. Capitals add emphasis that newer models tend to over-apply, and more reasoning does not tell the model what the label vocabulary is. (If the labels are a fixed set, a constrained output format also guarantees the shape.)

q: Last quarter a team estimated costs by assuming about 3.5 characters per token. After moving the same prompts to Claude Opus 5.5, bills run roughly 30 percent above that estimate, although request volume and prompt text are unchanged. What is the MOST likely explanation and best next step?
opts: Output tokens are billed at the input rate on newer models, so the cost model should drop its output term entirely and count input tokens only
The newer tokenizer produces more tokens for the same text, so recount with the token counting endpoint on the target model
Opus 5.5 silently adds a hidden system prompt to every API request, so ask support to remove it from the account
Prompt caching was switched off during the upgrade, so enable it again to restore last quarter's bill
why: Claude 4.7 and later models use a tokenizer that yields roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so counts, limits and bills measured on an older model must be re-baselined. The token counting endpoint takes the target model ID. The API adds no hidden system prompt, output tokens are still priced well above input tokens, and an upgrade never switches caching off.

q: A voice assistant on Claude Opus 5.5 streams its answers. Profiling shows the first token arrives after about 400 ms, but a 600-token answer then takes about 12 seconds to finish. The team can pay a premium for speed. Which option addresses the actual bottleneck?
opts: Raise max_tokens so that the model has room to finish the long answer more quickly
Add prompt caching to the system prompt, which shortens the wait before the first token appears
Enable fast mode on a model that supports it, which raises output tokens per second at premium pricing
Submit the requests through the Message Batches API, which gives higher throughput for large volumes
why: Latency has two parts: time to first token, driven by prompt length, model and any up-front reasoning, and generation speed in output tokens per second. The first token is already quick here, so generation speed is the bottleneck. Fast mode (on Opus 5.5, Opus 5 and Opus 4.8; research preview only on the last two) serves the same model at up to about 2.5 times the output speed for a higher price; it does not shorten the wait before the first token. Caching targets that first part, batch processing trades speed for a discount and cannot be combined with fast mode, and max_tokens is only a ceiling.

q: A summarization endpoint takes about 9 seconds per call. Each prompt has around 2,000 tokens, but the model writes about 1,500 tokens and the product needs only a three-sentence summary. Which change gives the BIGGEST latency improvement?
opts: Instruct the model to answer in three sentences, because output is generated token by token and its length drives the wait
Switch the call to the Message Batches API so the work is handled by a more efficient queue
Place a cache breakpoint on the prompt, because cache reads make every generated token arrive faster
Cut the 2,000-token prompt in half, because input and output tokens take the same time to process and the prompt is the larger of the two
why: Generation is autoregressive: the model produces one token after another, so after the first token, response time grows with output length. Asking for the short form (sentence or paragraph limits work better than word counts) removes about 1,400 generated tokens. Input is processed before the first token and mostly affects the time to first token, so halving it saves little. Caching reduces input cost and the first-token wait but not generation, and batch processing is for latency-tolerant work, not for faster answers.

q: A Node service calls the Messages API with hand-built HTTP requests. Engineers have repeatedly fixed missing version headers, absent retries on 429 and 5xx responses, and inconsistent timeouts. What is the MOST maintainable improvement?
opts: Send every request through the Message Batches API, which handles retries on the server side for the caller
Write a shared helper around the raw HTTP calls and ask engineers to use it for every new call from now on, checked in code review
Move the calls onto a WebSocket connection, which keeps the session open and avoids the need for retry logic
Adopt the official SDK, which sets the headers, retries transient errors with backoff and provides timeouts and typed errors
why: Client SDKs are thin wrappers around the REST API that already supply authentication, the required anthropic-version header, retries for connection errors, 429 and 5xx responses (two by default, honoring retry-after), timeouts, streaming helpers and error classes. A homemade helper recreates all of that and tends to drift. The Messages API is not a WebSocket interface, and the Batches API is asynchronous bulk processing rather than a reliability layer.

q: A chat web app must let users keep typing and cancel while a reply is still streaming. A developer proposes connecting the browser straight to the Claude API over a WebSocket. Which architecture is the BEST fit?
opts: Browser polling of the Messages API every second to fetch the partial text of the reply that is in progress
One non-streaming request held open until the full reply is ready, with cancellation handled by closing the tab
A WebSocket from the browser directly to the Claude API itself, with the API key stored in the page's JavaScript
A WebSocket between the browser and your own backend, which streams from the Messages API and relays the text
why: The Messages API streams over server-sent events on an ordinary HTTP response and has no WebSocket endpoint, and a browser must never hold the API key. A two-way channel between the browser and your own backend lets the user send messages and cancel while the backend consumes the event stream with the SDK and relays the text. There is no endpoint for polling a partial reply, and a non-streaming call returns only when it is complete.

q: A platform lets customers choose any Claude model. Some models accept thinking set to disabled and others return 400, and the lineup changes every few months. How should the code decide whether to send that setting?
opts: Keep a hard-coded table of model names and their settings in the code and update it by hand after every new release
Always send the setting, catch the 400 and retry without it on every single request
Assume each new model accepts exactly the settings of its predecessor and test only when users complain
Read the capabilities from the Models API and check whether disabling thinking is supported, rather than matching names
why: The Models API reports each model's capabilities, including whether thinking can be disabled, along with its maximum input and output sizes, so code can check support at runtime. A hand-maintained table goes stale, catching a 400 on every call wastes requests and hides the design flaw, and assuming parity is exactly what breaks across releases, as when disabling thinking is accepted on one model and rejected on another.

q: A legal-research tool sends whole case files to Claude. The largest files, over a million tokens, now fail with a 400 'prompt is too long', while smaller files work. Prompt caching is already enabled. What is the BEST way to handle the oversized files?
opts: Send only the relevant parts, using retrieval or summarization, because input beyond the window is rejected however it is cached
Add more cache breakpoints, because cached tokens do not count against the context window of the model
Set the thinking display to omitted so that reasoning tokens are removed from the window before the call
Raise max_tokens so that the response budget leaves enough space for the very long input in the window, which is shared with the reply
why: The context window is a hard limit on what a request can hold, and input alone beyond it is rejected with a 400. Prompt caching changes the price of repeated prefixes, not whether those tokens occupy the window. max_tokens only limits the output, and hiding thinking changes what you see, not how much input you send. Reduce the input: retrieve relevant passages, summarize or compact, or split the job across calls.

q: A fintech routes 40 million short support messages a month into twelve categories and needs a decision in well under a second. A prototype exists, but quality has not been measured. Which approach to model selection is BEST?
opts: Start with Claude Haiku 5.5, measure accuracy on a labeled sample of real messages, and move up only if the evals show a gap
Choose Claude Sonnet 5.5 for every message, because the middle tier is the safest default for any workload
Start with Claude Fable 5.1 so that accuracy is as high as possible, then see whether the bill is acceptable
Start with Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort and lower the effort only if finance complains about the cost
why: High-volume, latency-sensitive, well-defined work such as classification and routing is the case for efficiency-first selection: begin with the fastest, cheapest tier (Haiku 5.5), test on your own data and upgrade only for capability gaps the tests expose. Starting at the top is the capability-first path, suited to complex reasoning and high-stakes accuracy, and at this volume it would burn cost and latency before anything is known. A default tier chosen without measurement is a guess.

q: A research team's multi-hour agent reads hundreds of filings and writes a cited memo. On their eval set, Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh effort passes 71 percent of tasks against a 90 percent target, and prompt improvements have stalled. What is the BEST next step?
opts: Run the same eval set on Claude Fable 5.1, built for long-horizon work, and compare pass rate and cost per completed task
Lower effort to low on Opus 5.5 so that the model becomes more decisive about which filings to cite
Reduce the target to the 71 percent that the current model achieves and ship the agent as it stands
Switch to Claude Haiku 5.5, because the fastest tier lets the team iterate on the stalled prompt more quickly and run many more experiments
why: This is the documented capability-first path: start strong, optimize prompts, and if evals at xhigh or max effort still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work, move to Claude Fable 5.1, then confirm the gain and its cost on your own evals (and check its data-retention requirements). A smaller model or lower effort cuts capability on a task that is already failing, and lowering the target is not an engineering fix.

q: A document-analysis feature runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and meets its quality bar, but spend is 40 percent over budget. Engineers want to move all traffic to Claude Haiku 5.5 right away. What should the team do FIRST?
opts: Route a tenth of live traffic to Haiku 5.5 with no evals and watch the complaint rate for a week
Halve max_tokens so that every response is shorter and therefore cheaper to produce
Delete the system prompt to cut input tokens and keep the model and everything else unchanged
Run an effort sweep on the existing eval set, lowering effort step by step on Opus 5.5 while the pass rate holds
why: The docs note that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models: lower effort cuts thinking, tool calls and answer length while the model stays familiar, and a sweep on your own evals shows the cheapest level that still passes. Testing on customers instead of evals is risky; max_tokens only truncates a response and does not make the model economize (truncated output is still billed); deleting the system prompt would destroy the behavior the evals confirm.

q: A team wants to move a contract-clause extraction pipeline from Claude Sonnet 5.5 to a cheaper tier. Which evidence BEST supports the decision?
opts: A third party's published ranking of the model tiers on general coding benchmarks
Pass rates and cost per completed task for both models on an evaluation set of the team's own contracts and edge cases
The list price per million tokens of each model, since the cheaper one is cheaper for any pipeline, however many retries it needs
A manual check of five short, clean contracts that the engineers picked themselves
why: Anthropic's guidance: build benchmark tests specific to your use case (a good evaluation set is the most important step), test with your actual prompts and data, compare accuracy, quality and edge-case handling, then weigh cost. Per-token price ignores retries and extra turns, generic benchmarks may not resemble your contracts, and five hand-picked clean examples cannot reveal edge-case failures.

q: On a team's eval set, a smaller-tier model costs $0.30 per attempt and passes 40 percent of tasks; a larger-tier model costs $0.60 per attempt and passes 90 percent. Failed attempts are discarded and the task is attempted again until one passes. Which statement about expected cost per completed task is correct?
opts: The smaller tier is cheaper at about $0.12 per task against $0.54, because cost scales with the pass rate
The two tiers cost the same, because the higher price of the larger tier is exactly offset by its pass rate
The larger tier is cheaper: about $0.67 per completed task against $0.75 for the smaller tier
The smaller tier is cheaper, because $0.30 is half of $0.60 whatever the pass rates turn out to be
why: Expected attempts per solved task are 1 divided by the pass rate, so cost per completed task is cost per attempt divided by pass rate: 0.30 / 0.40 = $0.75 for the smaller tier and 0.60 / 0.90, about $0.67, for the larger. Comparing per-token or per-attempt prices ignores failures and retries, and multiplying cost by the pass rate gets the relationship backwards.

q: After switching an extraction service to Claude Sonnet 5.5, every request that forces a specific tool through tool_choice returns a 400, although it worked on the previous model. The team still needs tool inputs that always match the schema. What is the BEST change?
opts: Use tool_choice auto and turn on strict tool use for the tool, or request a JSON schema through structured outputs
Keep forcing the tool and wrap the call in a retry loop until the 400 stops appearing
Add a prefilled assistant turn that begins the tool call, so that the model has to continue it and cannot choose another tool
Set temperature to 0 so that the model reliably picks the only tool that is available to it
why: Forced tool use (tool_choice of type any or tool) is rejected on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1. The supported route is tool_choice auto, which the API accepts, combined with strict tool use so that tool inputs are schema-valid, or structured outputs when the reply itself must follow a schema. Prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later, non-default temperature is rejected on the current models, and a 400 is a request error that retries cannot cure.

q: A healthcare analytics company has a zero-data-retention arrangement with Anthropic. Its evals show only Claude Fable 5.1 meeting the quality bar on a hard reasoning workload. What should the team do BEFORE building on it?
opts: Rule out Fable 5.1 and drop to Haiku 5.5 so that the retention arrangement stays untouched
Check with compliance and Anthropic, because Fable models require 30-day retention and zero retention is unavailable for them
Enable Fable 5.1 as is, because zero data retention applies automatically to every model on the account, so no further check is needed
Route the requests through the Message Batches API, which never stores any request data on the server
why: Fable and Mythos models are Covered Models: they require 30-day data retention, so zero data retention is not available for them unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it, and an organization without the required setting can see requests rejected with a 400. This is a model-selection constraint to resolve first, by accepting the retention terms, seeking an exception, or tuning a model that fits the arrangement. The Batch API is stateful and not zero-retention eligible, and dropping to a much weaker tier ignores the quality bar the evals established.

q: A team runs a coding agent on a smaller executor model and gives it an advisor tool backed by a stronger model, hoping to cut cost while keeping quality on hard decisions. After a week, cost is down but hard-case quality has not improved. What should they check FIRST?
opts: Whether the advisor model's temperature is lower than the executor's on each consultation
How many cache breakpoints the executor's system prompt contains and where they are placed
How often the executor actually calls the advisor at hard decisions, which is the consult rate
Whether the advisor's context window is larger than the context window of the executor
why: The advisor pattern helps only when the executor consults the stronger model at the moments that matter. If it rarely does, the team pays for the extra tool definition (roughly a thousand prompt tokens on every request) and gets the smaller model's quality. Measure the consult rate, adjust the instructions, and compare the result with simply raising effort on one model. Sampling temperature is not adjustable on current models, and caching or window size does not decide whether the executor asks for help.

q: A support assistant sends the same 10,000-token policy prefix with every request, and it is sent 11 times within one five-minute window. Assume a five-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the base input price and a cache read costs 0.1 times it. How does the cost of the prefix compare with sending it uncached each time?
opts: About one and a quarter times as much, since every request pays the write price
About one tenth as much, since all 11 requests are billed as cache reads
About one fifth as much, since one write is followed by ten cheap reads
About nine tenths as much, since a cache read saves only ten percent
why: Uncached: 11 x 10,000 = 110,000 token-equivalents. Cached: one write at 1.25 x 10,000 = 12,500 plus ten reads at 0.1 x 10,000 = 1,000 each, so 10,000, for a total of 22,500, about 20 percent. Only the first request pays the write premium, and it does pay it, so not every request is a read; the later requests are not charged the write price; and a read costs a tenth of the base price, a 90 percent saving per read.

q: A tax-advice assistant caches a 30,000-token regulation excerpt. Users typically pause between 8 and 40 minutes between questions. The default five-minute cache lifetime is in use and cache reads are usually zero. What is the BEST change?
opts: Move the excerpt below the user's message so that the cache treats it as the newest content
Keep the five-minute lifetime and send a dummy request every four minutes, around the clock, to refresh each idle user's entry
Use the one-hour cache lifetime, accepting its higher write price, so that the prefix survives the users' pauses
Remove cache_control completely, since caching is never worthwhile when users pause between questions
why: A cache entry lives for five minutes from its last use, and each read refreshes it. With pauses of 8 to 40 minutes the entry has expired before the next turn, so every turn rewrites the prefix at the write price. The one-hour lifetime (written at twice the base input price, and paying off after two reads at the standard read rate) fits gaps between five minutes and an hour. Keep-alive pings add paid traffic for every idle user, moving content after the user message breaks the required prefix order of tools, system, then messages, and caching stays worthwhile whenever reuse within the lifetime is likely.

q: An assistant keeps one long conversation per user. To save money, the team sets effort to low on simple turns and high on complex ones, changing the top-level value from turn to turn. Cache reads fall sharply and spend rises. What is the MOST likely cause and best remedy?
opts: Cache entries are keyed to the exact wording of each user message, so normalize every message before it is sent
Each effort level is billed as a separate product, so the extra spend is simply the price of using two levels
Low effort disables prompt caching on that turn, so raise the minimum effort to medium for every turn of every conversation in the product
Changing effort invalidates the cached messages; keep it fixed per conversation or use per-message effort, which keeps the cache
why: Effort, like the thinking configuration, speed, tool_choice and images, is rendered into the prompt, so changing the top-level value starts a new cache prefix at the message layer and forces the conversation to be rewritten at the write price. Hold it constant, change it at a natural break such as right after a compaction, or use per-message effort (beta), which carries the change in a system message and leaves the cached prefix intact. Low effort does not disable caching, entries match on exact prefix content rather than on wording, and effort levels are not separate billing products.

q: A team picks Claude Haiku 5.5 as the cheapest model for summarizing long reports; each request carries about 300,000 tokens of input. Before projecting costs, what should they check?
opts: That requests above 200,000 tokens are rejected on Haiku 5.5, so the reports must be split in advance
That Haiku 5.5 charges more once a prompt passes 100,000 tokens, so compare cost per completed task with Sonnet 5.5 at this length
That thinking on Haiku 5.5 is billed as input, which changes the arithmetic for very long prompts
Nothing, because every current model bills a 1M-token request at the same per-token rate as a short one, so the lowest list price decides
why: Current models offer a 1M-token window, and most bill a long request at the same per-token rate as a short one. Claude Haiku 5.5 is the exception: it is priced by prompt length, and a prompt over 100,000 tokens (counting cache reads and writes) pays higher prices. A lower list price therefore does not guarantee the lowest cost at this size; compare cost per completed task at the real prompt length. The window applies to Haiku as well, and thinking is billed as output on every model.

q: Finance wants monthly spend broken down by product feature and by environment, and engineering wants to see cache efficiency per model. Which setup BEST supports this?
opts: Separate workspaces per feature and environment, queried through the Usage and Cost API with an admin credential, grouped by workspace and model
One organization-wide key shared by every service, with each developer recording token counts by hand in a spreadsheet
Parsing the monthly invoice and dividing its total by the number of requests that each team believes it sent
Character-count estimates stored next to every request and summed per feature at the end of each month
why: The Usage and Cost API reports token usage and cost in time buckets that can be filtered and grouped by model, workspace, API key and service tier, which also supports cache-efficiency analysis; it needs an admin-level credential rather than a normal workspace key. Giving each feature and environment its own workspace makes attribution a simple group-by (and isolates limits and caches). Hand-kept counts, invoice splitting and character-based estimates are inaccurate and cannot show cache or model differences.

q: An autonomous agent makes dozens of tool calls. It sometimes exhausts its output allowance in the middle of a step and leaves work half done. The team wants the model to pace itself and wrap up gracefully within a total allowance for the whole loop. Which control fits BEST?
opts: A larger context window, because running out of window is the only way a loop can end early
A smaller max_tokens, so that the model notices the limit and economizes as it works
A higher effort level, because thorough models always finish before they reach any limit
A task budget, an advisory allowance for the whole agentic loop that the model sees as a running countdown
why: max_tokens caps a single response and is invisible to the model, so reaching it truncates the work mid-step (and the discarded turn is still billed). A task budget (beta) is advisory: the model sees a countdown across the whole loop and can prioritize and finish cleanly. Effort scales thoroughness per step rather than total length, and the window size is unrelated to the allowance.

q: An internal tool resends a 15,000-token style guide and tool list with every request, thousands of times a day, to a model that already meets its quality targets. Which optimization saves the MOST with NO quality tradeoff?
opts: Move to the next smaller model tier and accept the small drop in accuracy that the team measured on its own evals
Cap max_tokens at a small number so that responses are cut off early
Enable prompt caching on the stable prefix so that repeated reads cost a fraction of the normal input price
Lower effort one level for every request, regardless of how hard each one is, and accept some loss
why: Caching cuts the cost and latency of repeated input without changing what the model produces, so the docs count it among the free wins and it is usually the largest. A smaller tier, a lower effort and output caps are tradeoffs: each can cost quality, and a tight max_tokens truncates replies, wasting the tokens already generated.

q: Which TWO statements about getting consistent output from Claude Opus 5.5 are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Raising top_k widens the pool of candidate tokens, which makes repeated runs of one request more alike
Prefilling the opening words of the reply is the recommended way to lock its wording
A JSON schema supplied through structured outputs removes variation in the shape of the reply, though not in its wording
Non-default temperature, top_p and top_k are rejected with a 400, so consistency comes from prompts, examples and output constraints
Setting temperature to 0 makes repeated identical requests return byte-identical text on every run
why: Current models reject non-default sampling parameters, so consistency is engineered through clear instructions, varied examples, structured outputs (a schema-guaranteed shape) and effort. Structured outputs fix the form, not the wording. Temperature 0 never guaranteed identical text, a wider top_k would increase variety rather than reduce it (and is rejected anyway), and prefill is rejected with a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later models.

q: Which TWO statements about thinking tokens on current Claude models are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Setting the display to omitted removes the cost of the reasoning from the bill
They are free whenever the prompt prefix was served from the cache
They are billed as output tokens even when the response omits the thinking text
They count toward max_tokens, so a low ceiling at high effort can leave no room for the visible answer
A summarized display is billed at the length of the summary rather than the reasoning that was generated
why: Thinking is billed as output and counts against max_tokens whether or not the text is returned. A summarized display is a readable summary produced separately; you are charged for the full thinking tokens, not the summary. Caching affects input pricing only, and omitting the display changes only what is returned (it can improve time to first text token when streaming), not what is billed.

q: Which THREE changes between two requests invalidate a cached prefix that covers the tools, the system prompt and the conversation so far? (Choose three.)
opts: Appending a new user message after the last cache breakpoint of the conversation
Changing the top-level effort value between the two requests
Sending the next request 90 seconds after the last one, inside the five-minute lifetime
Inserting a per-request timestamp into the system prompt
Editing the wording of one tool's description
why: The cache is a prefix in the order tools, system, messages, matched exactly, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. Tool edits clear everything, a system edit or a speed change clears the system and messages layers, and effort, thinking, tool_choice or image changes clear the messages layer. New content after the last breakpoint is simply new input, and a read inside the lifetime refreshes the entry rather than invalidating it.

q: A team wants to cut the bill of a stable workload without lowering answer quality. Which TWO measures qualify? (Choose two.)
opts: Set max_tokens to a small value so that replies stop early
Move every request to the next smaller model tier
Lower effort one level across the board without running evals
Send non-urgent work, such as a nightly evaluation run, through the Message Batches API
Cache the large prefix that repeats across requests
why: Caching repeated input and batching work that can wait up to 24 hours (half price on input and output) cut cost without changing what the model produces. Moving to a smaller tier, lowering effort and capping output are tradeoffs that may reduce quality, so they need evals first; a tight max_tokens truncates replies and wastes the tokens already generated.

q: A team is building a pre-launch cost model for a multi-turn assistant that calls tools. Which THREE items belong in the estimate? (Choose three.)
opts: Only the length of the user's visible messages, since everything else is free
A flat fee per request that does not depend on the number of tokens
Tool definitions and the tool-use overhead added to every request
Thinking tokens, which are billed at the output rate
The conversation history that is resent as input on every turn
why: The Messages API is stateless, so the whole history is sent again each turn and input grows with conversation length; tool definitions, tool_use and tool_result blocks and the special tool-use system prompt all count as input tokens; reasoning is billed as output. Then adjust for cache hits and batch discounts, and recount for the target model's tokenizer. Charging is per token rather than a flat fee, and history, system prompts and tool results are far from free.

q: A team is moving production code from an older model to Claude Opus 5.5. Which THREE changes should they expect to make? (Choose three.)
opts: Add a prefilled assistant message so that the reply is forced to start with an opening brace
Recount prompts with the token counting endpoint, because the tokenizer yields more tokens for the same text
Remove non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values
Send thinking disabled to cut cost on simple requests
Replace manual thinking budgets with adaptive thinking and an effort setting
why: Opus 5.5 rejects non-default sampling parameters and the manual budget_tokens mode, and the tokenizer introduced with Claude 4.7 produces roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so counts and cost estimates must be redone. Prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later, and thinking cannot be disabled on Opus 5.5, so both of those would return a 400.

q: A nightly job scores 40,000 documents against the same 12,000-token rubric, and the results are needed by morning. Which TWO measures together lower the cost MOST? (Choose two.)
opts: Submit the work through the Message Batches API for the half-price discount on input and output
Lower max_tokens to one token for every document in the job
Send the requests synchronously in parallel so that the cache is warm for all of them at once
Put the rubric in a cached prefix with the one-hour lifetime, because the batch and caching discounts stack
Request fast mode for the job so that it finishes earlier, at premium prices
why: Batch processing is 50 percent off both input and output and suits work that can wait up to 24 hours; caching a shared prefix stacks with that discount (cache hits inside a batch are best-effort, so the one-hour lifetime is recommended). Parallel synchronous calls get no batch discount, and a cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins, so simultaneous requests may all miss. Fast mode costs a premium and is not available with the Batch API, and a one-token output cannot score anything.

q: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees that Claude returns identical text for identical requests.
opts: True
False
why: Output can vary between calls even with low randomness settings, and current models reject non-default temperature anyway. Tests and pipelines should tolerate variation and validate outputs in code.

q: Claude Opus 5.5 accepts thinking type disabled as a way to switch reasoning off for simple requests.
opts: True
False
why: Adaptive thinking is always on for Opus 5.5 (and Fable 5.1), and sending disabled returns a 400. Lower the effort level to reduce reasoning. Some other models do accept disabling it, which is why code should read capabilities from the Models API.

q: Fast mode raises output speed in tokens per second but does not shorten the wait before the first token appears.
opts: True
False
why: Fast mode serves the same model with a faster inference setup, up to about 2.5 times the output speed at premium pricing, on some Opus models. Time to first token is driven by prompt length, model choice and up-front reasoning, so shorter prompts and caching address that part.

q: Prompt caching lowers the price of a repeated prefix, but the cached tokens still count toward the context window.
opts: True
False
why: Caching changes what you pay and how fast the prefix is processed, not whether the tokens occupy the window. A request whose input exceeds the window is rejected however much of it is cached.

q: Writing a prefix to the five-minute cache costs more than sending it uncached, so caching a prompt that is never reused within five minutes raises the bill.
opts: True
False
why: A five-minute write costs about 1.25 times the base input price and the saving comes only from later reads, at a tenth of the price or less. Without reuse inside the lifetime there are no reads, so you only pay the premium. Check the cache usage fields to confirm hits.

q: On Claude Sonnet 5.5, a 900,000-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9,000-token request.
opts: True
False
why: The 1M-token window is included at standard pricing on Claude 4.6 and later models. Claude Haiku 5.5 is the exception, because it is priced higher for prompts over 100,000 tokens.

q: A smaller model tier always costs less per completed task than a larger tier.
opts: True
False
why: Cost per completed task includes retries, extra turns and failed attempts. A pricier model that passes more often or finishes in fewer turns can be cheaper per solved task, so measure on your own evals instead of comparing price lists.

q: The effort setting also influences tool use: at lower levels Claude tends to make fewer and terser tool calls.
opts: True
False
why: Effort affects all tokens in a reply, including text, tool calls with their arguments, and thinking when it is active. Lower effort saves cost and time, but on long agent tasks it can mean skipped searches or checks, so validate on evals.

q: All current Claude models share the same default effort level.
opts: True
False
why: The default is high on most models but medium on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, and setting the default explicitly is the same as omitting the parameter. Set effort explicitly when moving between models and sweep it on your evals.

q: A cache breakpoint belongs on the last block that stays identical across the requests meant to share a cache, not on content that changes with every request.
opts: True
False
why: Cache writes happen only at breakpoints and the prefix up to the breakpoint must match exactly. A breakpoint on a timestamp or on per-request context never matches, so every request pays a fresh write and never reads.

q: A prompt shorter than the minimum cacheable length that carries a cache_control marker is rejected with an error.
opts: True
False
why: It is processed normally without caching and no error is returned; both cache counts in the usage object show zero. The minimum is 512 tokens on the current models, and padding a prompt that sits just under it with stable content can lower the cost of frequently reused prompts.

q: Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens on the current models, so asking for a concise reply can save more than trimming the prompt by the same number of tokens.
opts: True
False
why: Output is priced at five times input on the current models, and in an agent loop the generated text is re-read as input on later turns. Asking for the answer you will actually read is a cheap, effective lever.

q: A triage tool sends each support ticket to Claude with the prompt "Summarize this ticket." Summaries range from one line to a full page, and the routing code that reads them cannot rely on any structure. Which change is BEST?
opts: Add the word IMPORTANT in capital letters and ask the model to be consistent every time
Run each ticket three times and keep whichever of the summaries turns out to be the shortest
Name the reader and purpose, and fix the fields and length: symptom, component and impact in three sentences
Truncate every summary to its first 200 characters before it is passed to the routing code
why: The prompt leaves the audience, content and shape to guesswork, so a capable colleague without context would have to guess as well. Naming the reader and fixing the fields and length removes the variance at its source. Capital letters add pressure but no information, picking the shortest of three runs triples the cost and still guesses the structure, and truncation cuts content arbitrarily.

q: A sentiment classifier prompt contains four worked examples, all labelled positive, written inside the paragraph of instructions. In production it labels nearly every review positive and sometimes copies phrasing from the examples. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Replace the examples with a longer written description of positive reviews and leave the negative cases to general knowledge
Provide varied examples that cover every label and the tricky edge cases, each in its own example tags
Repeat the same four examples a second time so that the model gives them more weight
Strip the labels from the examples so that the model has to infer the answers itself
why: Examples teach by pattern, so a one-sided set teaches a one-sided habit. Varied examples that span every label and the hard cases, kept in tags that separate them from the instructions, fix both the bias and the copying. A prose description does not show the boundary between labels, duplicating a biased set amplifies it, and unlabeled examples remove the very thing they were meant to demonstrate.

q: An HR assistant answers questions from about 60 policy documents, roughly 150,000 tokens in all. The prompt begins with the employee's question and then pastes the documents with no markers, and answers often miss details buried in the middle. Which restructure is BEST?
opts: Put the documents first in source-labeled tags, the question last, and ask for relevant quotes before the answer
Move the question into the middle of the documents so that it sits as close as possible to the relevant text, wherever that is
Compress every document to a fifty-word summary first and send only the summaries to keep the prompt short
Repeat the employee's question at the start of every document so that the model never loses track of it
why: For long inputs, put the documents near the top and the question or instructions at the end. Tagging each document with its source lets the model point to it, and asking for word-for-word quotes first focuses attention on the relevant passages. Hiding the question inside the text, over-compressing the documents and repeating the question dozens of times all add noise or throw detail away.

q: A chat widget needs short answers. The prompt asks for "no more than 120 words" and max_tokens is set to 160, yet many replies still run long and some stop in the middle of a sentence. What is the BEST approach?
opts: Lower max_tokens to 80 so that every reply is forced to stay inside the widget
Raise the temperature so that the model is less likely to keep repeating itself at length
Ask the model to count its words after writing and to rewrite any answer that is over the limit
Ask for two to three sentences in the prompt and keep max_tokens as a safety ceiling well above that
why: The model works in pieces of text rather than words, so sentence or paragraph limits are followed more closely than word counts. max_tokens is a hard ceiling that cuts text off wherever it falls, so it belongs behind the prompt as a safety net, not in front of it as the length control. Lowering it makes truncation worse, randomness settings do not govern length, and a count-and-rewrite pass spends extra output tokens on an unreliable check.

q: A prompt says: "Do not use markdown. Do not use bullet points. Never use headings." The system prompt itself is full of markdown headings and lists, and replies still arrive as bullet lists. Which change is MOST likely to fix this?
opts: Repeat the three prohibitions in capital letters at the very end of the user message
Rewrite the prompt in plain prose and state the target, such as "write in flowing paragraphs, like a short email"
