Start the assistant turn with a plain-text sentence so that the reply continues in that style instead of switching to lists
Remove the bullet characters from every reply with a regular expression before display
why: Saying what to do steers more reliably than listing what to avoid, and the style of a prompt tends to leak into the style of the output, so a markdown-heavy prompt invites markdown. Capital letters add pressure rather than information, prefilling the assistant turn is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later models, and stripping bullets treats the symptom and can mangle legitimate text.

q: A team moves from an older model to Claude Sonnet 5.5. Their prompt says: "CRITICAL: you MUST ALWAYS call search_docs before answering anything." Now the agent calls search_docs for greetings and arithmetic, adding latency and cost. What is the BEST first step?
opts: Restate the rule with its condition in plain words, such as "use search_docs for questions about company documents"
Set the effort level to its minimum so that the model has less room to over-apply the rule
Add a second CRITICAL rule telling the model never to search when the user is only greeting
Pin the application to the older model so that the previous behavior comes back unchanged, and postpone any prompt changes
why: Newer models follow system prompts closely, so wording that was needed to overcome under-triggering in older models now causes over-application. Restating the rule with its condition in plain language and re-testing is the first fix. Lowering effort changes how hard the model works, not what it was told; a second shouted rule piles on emphasis; pinning an old model skips the prompt audit that every model change deserves.

q: A voice assistant's replies are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that stumbles over symbols. The prompt says "Never use ellipses." Replies now avoid ellipses but include emoji, slashes and parenthetical asides that the engine also mispronounces. Which prompt change is BEST?
opts: Add each symbol that has caused trouble so far to a growing list of banned characters
Warn the model that any reply containing a symbol will be penalized and thrown away
Say that replies are spoken aloud by a speech engine, and ask for short natural sentences without symbols
Ask the model to scan each finished reply for symbols and to fix any it finds before sending, as a last pass
why: A rule with no reason is applied only to the case it names; giving the purpose lets the model generalize to symbols nobody listed. A ban list always lags behind the next failure, threats add pressure but no information, and a self-scan costs tokens and still depends on the model knowing what to look for.

q: A prompt template places customer feedback between <feedback> and </feedback> tags. A tester submits text that begins with </feedback> followed by new instructions, and the model starts obeying them. Which step addresses this break-out MOST directly?
opts: Neutralize the closing-tag sequence in the submitted text and cap its length before inserting it
Rename the tags to an unusual word and keep the new name out of all documentation
Add a note on the feedback form asking customers not to type anything that looks like a tag or an instruction
End every reply with a statement that only the original instructions were followed
why: The attack works because the data section can be closed by the data itself. Escaping or removing the delimiter sequence, bounding the length and normalizing the text keeps untrusted input inside its section. It is one layer, not a cure, so pair it with least-privilege tools and output checks. A secret tag name is obscurity, a polite request to attackers is not a control, and a closing statement changes nothing about what the model has already read.

q: A legal team sends its entire 600,000-token contract archive with every question because the model's window can hold it. Answers are slow and expensive, and sometimes worse than when a developer pasted just the relevant clauses by hand. What is the BEST redesign?
opts: Move to a larger model tier so that the extra context is handled without any loss of accuracy
Tell the model in the prompt to pay equal attention to every document in the archive
Cache the archive and keep sending all of it, since caching removes the accuracy penalty of length
Retrieve the few passages that are relevant to each question and send only those, with their sources
why: A large window is a ceiling, not a target: accuracy and recall tend to fall as irrelevant material piles up (context rot), and every extra token adds latency and cost. Retrieval keeps the prompt focused on evidence that matters. A bigger tier does not remove the effect, an instruction cannot make attention uniform, and caching lowers the price of repeated tokens while they still occupy the window.

q: A research agent runs for hours. Its history is dominated by old web-page tool results that are no longer needed, while its own findings and decisions must stay word for word. Which feature fits BEST?
opts: Compaction, replacing all older turns with a model-written summary of the whole session
Context editing, clearing the oldest tool results by rule and leaving placeholders behind
Prompt caching on the full history so that the old results cost less to resend each turn
A lower max_tokens value so that fewer tokens are carried over into later turns
why: Tool result clearing targets exactly the stale bulk and leaves everything else untouched. Compaction summarizes the older turns, so findings and decisions would be paraphrased and details lost. Caching changes the price of the repeated prefix, not the space it occupies, and max_tokens caps one reply, not the history.

q: A migration agent works through 300 database tables over several hours, and its context is compacted twice. Afterwards it repeats tables it already converted and skips others. What is the MOST reliable improvement?
opts: Ask the model to remember the finished tables more carefully after each compaction
Turn compaction off so that the early messages stay in context however long the run lasts
Keep a structured progress file of finished tables that the agent updates and re-reads as it works
Process fewer tables per session and let the compaction summary carry the rest of the list between sessions
why: Exact state is a poor fit for a model-written summary, which is lossy by design. A small structured file, ideally alongside version control, is durable, cheap to re-read and precise, and it survives compaction or a fresh session. Asking the model to try harder cannot restore details that were summarized away, switching compaction off eventually overflows the window, and leaning on the summary repeats the original weakness.

q: One long prompt asks Claude to read 30 vendor contracts, extract every termination clause, draft a risk memo and then critique its own memo. Quality drops in the later steps, and the critique tends to repeat the memo's mistakes. Which redesign is BEST?
opts: Split it into separate calls: extract per contract, draft the memo from the structured clauses, review in a fresh context
Keep the single prompt but add an instruction to think carefully, double-check each step and critique the memo as harshly as possible
Run the identical prompt five times and keep the memo that most of the runs agree with
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that every contract and all four steps can stay in one call
why: A multi-step workflow gives each step a clean context: extraction runs per contract (and can run in parallel), only structured results move forward, and the reviewer sees the memo without the author's reasoning, so it can catch errors instead of inheriting them. Added caution, voting among identical runs and a bigger window all leave one crowded context in place.

q: A coding agent must work in a monorepo with millions of lines. A proposal is to generate a summary of every directory and load all of it into the system prompt at the start of each session. What is the BEST alternative?
opts: Split the repository into chunks and send the chunks on a rotating schedule over successive turns
Paste the whole repository into the first user message and rely on prompt caching to keep the cost of later turns down
Ask the model to memorize the directory summaries and then drop them from the prompt after turn one
Give the agent search and file-reading tools plus path conventions, so it loads detail only when a task needs it
why: Lightweight handles such as paths and queries, plus tools to open them, let an agent explore the way an engineer does: find what matters, read it, move on. Preloading everything fills the window with mostly irrelevant material that also goes stale. Rotating chunks or a cached giant paste still occupy the window, and a model cannot memorize text it no longer sees.

q: A support chatbot keeps only the last ten messages of each conversation to control cost. After a long chat it forgets the account number and the problem the customer described at the start. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Keep a running summary of older turns plus a pinned block of durable facts, such as the account number
Raise the cutoff to the last forty messages and accept the higher cost for every conversation
Ask customers to repeat their account number whenever the assistant seems to have forgotten it
Store the full transcript in a database and expect the model to recall it from there on its own when it needs it
why: Dropping old turns loses exactly the facts that were set early. A summary of older turns plus a pinned block of durable facts is cheap and survives trimming. A longer cutoff only postpones the problem, asking customers to repeat themselves pushes the work onto them, and a database helps only if the application actually puts the content into the request, because the model sees nothing else.

q: An invoice extractor uses structured outputs, so every reply parses. Still, about 2 percent of results have a total that does not equal the sum of the line items. What is the BEST way to handle this?
opts: Add "be careful with arithmetic" to the prompt and treat the problem as solved
Check the totals in code, re-prompt once with the exact discrepancy on a mismatch, then escalate to a person
Turn structured outputs off, since constrained decoding is what introduces the arithmetic errors, and parse free text instead
Resend the same request unchanged until the totals happen to match
why: A schema guarantees shape, not truth. Business rules such as lines summing to the total belong in code, and feeding the exact violation back usually fixes the reply. Capping the attempts and escalating keeps failures visible and cost bounded. A reminder in the prompt is a wish, constrained decoding does not cause arithmetic errors, and blind retries burn money without adding information.

q: A policy Q&A bot sometimes invents rules that are not in the 200-page handbook it is given. Which prompt design reduces this MOST?
opts: Ask it to state a confidence percentage and show a warning to users when the number is low
Tell it to avoid expressing doubt and to always give a definite answer so that users trust the bot
Restrict it to the handbook, make it quote supporting passages first, and let it say when the handbook is silent
Let it use general knowledge when the handbook is silent, marking those answers with the word "estimate" so that users can judge them
why: Grounding techniques cut invented claims: limit the model to the supplied text, make it extract quotes before it answers, and give it explicit permission to say the answer is not there. A self-reported percentage is not calibrated evidence, forcing a definite answer pushes toward invention, and licensing general knowledge reopens the gap. These techniques reduce hallucination but cannot eliminate it, so critical answers still need checks.

q: A research assistant answers with quoted passages from uploaded reports. A reviewer finds a quote that appears nowhere in the report it is attributed to. Which safeguard is MOST effective against this?
opts: Ask the model, at the end of each answer, to confirm that every quote is accurate and appears in the report
Add "never fabricate quotes" to the system prompt in emphatic wording
Ask for longer answers with more quotes so that errors become easier to spot by eye
Check in code that each quote occurs in the cited source, and withdraw any claim whose quote does not
why: A mechanical check against the source is independent of the model's confidence: a quote that cannot be found is rejected. The citations feature, which returns pointers to the exact supporting passages in your documents, serves the same purpose. A confirmation from the same model shares its blind spots, a prohibition is still only a request, and more quotes mean more to verify.

q: A contracts tool must return a parseable verdict (approve, review or reject) and also ground its statements with citations to the supplied contract. A single request with both citations and structured outputs enabled returns a 400 error. Which design BEST works within this limit?
opts: Keep both features on and retry the request with exponential backoff until it succeeds
Call once with citations for the grounded analysis, then again to convert that analysis into the verdict schema
Drop citations and ask for sources in free text, which the code extracts with a regular expression before storing the verdict
Keep structured outputs and add an optional string field in the schema where the model writes its citations
why: The two features cannot be combined in one request, and a 400 is a request error that retrying will not fix. Splitting the work lets each feature do what it is good at: verifiable pointers to the source passages in one step, a schema-conforming verdict in the next. Free-text sources and a schema field of model-written strings lose the verifiable pointers that citations provide.

q: An approval workflow asks Claude to rate its confidence from 0 to 100 and automatically approves anything above 90. A later audit finds several confident approvals that were wrong. What is the BEST correction?
opts: Raise the approval threshold to 99 so that only the most confident answers pass automatically
Ask the model to rate its confidence twice and average the two numbers before applying the threshold, so one noisy rating matters less
Rely on checks you can verify, such as rules and tests in code and sampled human review, not self-rating alone
Instruct the model to be more humble so that its confidence numbers become better calibrated
why: A fluent, assured answer and a high self-rating are not evidence of correctness. Anchor decisions on independent verification and scale the review to the stakes. A higher threshold or an average only rescales an unreliable signal, and telling the model to be humble does not calibrate it.

q: Which TWO items belong in the system prompt of a customer-support assistant rather than in the user turn? (Choose two.)
opts: The text of the customer's current message, which changes on every turn
The assistant's role and the escalation policy that apply to every conversation
The contents of the order record retrieved for this particular customer
The tone and formatting rules that every reply must follow
The specific question to be answered about that order today
why: The system prompt carries what is stable across turns: the role, the policies and the output rules. The current message, the retrieved record and today's question change per request and belong in the user turn, where untrusted customer text also gets less authority than the system prompt. A fixed system prompt is also easier to cache.

q: A team moves its prompts to a newer model. Which TWO edits belong in a sensible prompt audit? (Choose two.)
opts: Remove hand-built scratchpad steps and "verify everything twice" rules that compensated for an older model
Add a prefilled assistant opening so that the output format stays steady
Replace shouted MUST and CRITICAL wording with plain statements of when to act
Add more capital-letter emphasis so that the old behavior is preserved exactly
Delete every example, since newer models never benefit from demonstrations
why: Newer models follow instructions more literally and bring their own reasoning, so compensating text now causes extra work or over-application. The audit removes it and re-runs the evaluation set. Prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later models, extra emphasis worsens over-triggering, and examples remain one of the strongest tools for fixing format.

q: Which THREE practices keep the context of a tool-heavy agent from filling with stale bulk? (Choose three.)
opts: Return only the fields the next step needs from each tool, and paginate large lists
Keep every raw tool response in the history in case the model wants to re-read it later
Clear the oldest tool results by rule once the history passes a size threshold
Delegate noisy side investigations to a subagent that returns a short conclusion
Raise max_tokens so that the window is counted as having more room
why: Lean tool outputs, rule-based clearing and isolating side work all keep the working context small, and the cheapest fix is not producing the bulk in the first place. Keeping every raw response is the problem itself, and max_tokens bounds one reply, not the accumulated history.

q: A bot answers questions about supplied technical manuals. Which TWO prompt changes reduce unsupported claims? (Choose two.)
opts: Ask for a confident, authoritative tone so that users trust the result
Allow the explicit answer that the manual does not contain the information
Tell it to fill gaps from general knowledge whenever a manual is silent
Have it extract word-for-word quotes from the manuals first and answer using only those quotes
Put the question before the manuals so that it is not influenced by the long documents
why: Permission to say the answer is not in the manuals removes the pressure to invent, and quote-first answering ties each claim to text that exists. A confident tone encourages bluffing, filling gaps from general knowledge reopens the gap, and for long documents the stronger structure puts the manuals first and the question last.

q: Explaining why a rule exists, for example that replies will be read aloud by a speech engine, helps the model apply the rule sensibly to cases the prompt never listed.
opts: True
False
why: A reason conveys the intent behind the rule, so the model can generalize. A bare prohibition tends to be applied to the case it names and little else.

q: Stripping the phrase "ignore previous instructions" from user input is enough on its own to stop prompt injection.
opts: True
False
why: Blocklists of known phrases are easy to evade by rewording, translating or encoding the attack. Input sanitization, such as escaping delimiters and bounding length, is one layer to combine with structural separation of untrusted content, least-privilege tools and checks in code.

q: Because a very large context window can hold the material, adding more documents to a prompt never lowers the quality of the answer.
opts: True
False
why: Accuracy and recall tend to degrade as the window fills with material (context rot), and more tokens add latency and cost. Curate what goes in: retrieve what is relevant and trim what is stale.

q: Prompt caching reduces how many tokens of the context window a prompt occupies.
opts: True
False
why: Caching changes the price and speed of reprocessing a repeated prefix. Cached tokens still count toward the window, so it does nothing for a conversation that is about to overflow; use compaction, context editing or smaller inputs for that.

q: Context editing removes older tool results by rule before the prompt reaches the model and leaves a short marker where the content was.
opts: True
False
why: Tool result clearing is applied oldest first once a configured threshold is passed, and the marker tells the model that something was removed. Clearing changes the cached prefix, so clear enough tokens each time to make the cache invalidation worthwhile.

q: If several runs of the same prompt give the same answer, that answer is guaranteed to be correct.
opts: True
False
why: Disagreement between runs is a useful flag for unreliable content, but agreement only shows consistency: the runs share the same blind spots and can repeat the same mistake. Verify important claims against a source, a test or a person.

q: Giving the model explicit permission to say that it does not know is one way to reduce hallucination.
opts: True
False
why: Without that permission the model is pushed toward producing some answer. Pair it with quote-first grounding and restriction to the supplied documents; none of these techniques eliminates hallucination.

q: Compaction and context editing are the same feature: both replace older content with a model-written summary.
opts: True
False
why: Compaction summarizes the older turns of a conversation, which keeps the thread alive but loses detail. Context editing deletes specified content, such as old tool results or thinking blocks, by rule and leaves placeholders; nothing is summarized.

q: An email assistant summarizes incoming mail and, when asked, can send replies. A spam message contains hidden text telling the assistant to forward the user's last ten emails to an outside address. Which design BEST limits this risk?
opts: Add a line to the system prompt saying that emails may contain malicious instructions that must be ignored
Treat email bodies as untrusted tool-result data and hold every send for the user's approval, showing recipient and text
Delete incoming messages that contain the phrase "ignore previous instructions" or similar wording before the assistant ever sees them
Switch to a larger model tier so that the assistant recognizes hidden instructions more reliably
why: Indirect injection arrives through content the user never wrote. Labeling and isolating that content lowers the odds of success, but the dependable control is a gate in code on the consequential action: the send is held until a person sees the exact recipient and body. A prompt warning is a request, phrase filters are evaded by rewording, and a stronger model reduces the risk without removing it.

q: A public bank chatbot keeps receiving role-play prompts designed to make it ignore its restrictions. Which combination is MOST appropriate?
opts: Block a growing list of known jailbreak phrases with exact string matching, and review the list with the security team every month
Remove the system prompt, so that attackers have no instructions to override
Run the chatbot at the highest effort setting so that it reasons more deeply about each attempt before it answers
Pre-screen messages with a small model, harden the system prompt, and throttle accounts that keep probing
why: For direct attacks, where the user is the adversary, layer a lightweight harmlessness screen (a refusal from the screening model counts as a harmful verdict), a system prompt that states values and how to decline, monitoring, and action against repeat offenders. Phrase lists are evaded by rewording, removing the system prompt removes your guardrails, and more reasoning effort is a cost setting, not a security control.

q: A support portal renders Claude's replies by inserting them straight into the page's HTML. A researcher plants text in a public forum post that the assistant reads, and the assistant's next reply contains a script tag that runs in other users' browsers. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Treat the reply as untrusted: escape or sanitize it before rendering and block active content
Tell the model in the system prompt never to output HTML tags, scripts or links of any kind in its replies
Ask the model to check its own reply for scripts and to rewrite it before returning it to the portal
Block the assistant from reading that one forum domain and leave everything else as it is today
why: Model output can be steered by anything the model reads, so it must be handled like any untrusted input at the point of use: encode it for the destination (HTML escaping or a sanitizer), disallow executable content, and do not render remote images or links automatically, since those can carry data out. Prompt instructions and self-checks are not guarantees, and blocking one domain fixes only this instance.

q: A claims tool sends complete customer records, including full names, government ID numbers and addresses, to Claude to draft a one-paragraph summary, and it logs every prompt for debugging. Which change is BEST?
opts: Tell the model in the prompt never to repeat the ID numbers or addresses in its summary, and check that it complies
Keep sending everything but use the newest version of the transport encryption protocol
Send only the fields the summary needs, mask identifiers with placeholders, and keep them out of the logs
Keep sending everything and rely on the provider's retention settings to cover the logs
why: Data you never send cannot leak from a prompt, a response, a cache or your own logs. Minimizing and masking personal data before the call, and keeping it out of debug logs, closes all of those paths. An instruction only governs the output, transport encryption is already expected, and the provider's retention terms do not govern what your own systems store.

q: A retail chatbot's system prompt contains a staff-only discount code and the key for an internal pricing service. Users have begun extracting the prompt with clever questions. What is the BEST response?
opts: Add a firm instruction to the prompt never to reveal its contents under any circumstances
Remove the secrets from the prompt, keep the key in server-side tool code, and screen the replies
Encode the discount code and the key in base64 so that they are no longer readable to casual users of the chatbot
Mix decoy codes into the prompt so that a leaked value is harder to identify as the real one
why: No wording makes it impossible for a model to repeat text it can see, so anything in a prompt must be assumed disclosable: keep secrets out, and put credentials where only your code can reach them. Monitoring and filtering outputs can catch leaks. A firmer instruction is still a request, base64 is encoding rather than protection (the model can decode it), and decoys leave the real values exposed.

q: A reporting agent needs to read three tables. Its run_sql tool connects with the database administrator account, and the system prompt says "Only run SELECT statements." Which change is BEST?
opts: Connect the tool with a role that has read-only rights on just those three tables
Add a regular expression to the tool that rejects statements containing DROP or DELETE
Rewrite the system prompt rule in capital letters and repeat it in the tool description
Review the query log once a week and revoke access if a write statement is found
why: Least privilege removes the capability instead of asking for restraint: even a successful injection or a model error cannot write, or read other tables. A keyword blocklist is incomplete and easy to bypass, emphasis is still a request, and a weekly review detects damage only after it has happened.

q: A data-analysis agent runs Python code that the model writes, on a shared application server whose process environment holds the cloud credentials for the whole product. Which setup is BEST?
opts: Scan the generated code for suspicious function names and run it on the server if none are found in the scan results
Ask a second model to review each script and approve it before it runs on the shared server
Run the code on the server under the same account, since the model was told to write safe code
Run the code in an isolated container or VM with no credentials and outbound traffic limited to an allowlist
why: Model-written code is untrusted code. Isolation (a container, a user-space kernel such as gVisor, or a virtual machine) with minimal mounts, no credentials and an egress allowlist contains a mistake or an injected instruction no matter what the code does. Static scans and model reviewers miss obfuscated behavior, and an instruction to be safe is not a boundary.

q: A ticket-handling agent can look up orders, add internal notes, issue refunds and delete accounts. Product wants a person to approve every single tool call, but reviewers are already clicking approve without reading. What is the BEST adjustment?
opts: Keep approving every call but add a daily summary email of what was approved
Remove approvals entirely and ask the agent in the system prompt to be careful with refunds, deletions and anything else that looks risky
Run read-only and reversible steps automatically, and hold refunds and deletions for approval showing the exact target
Approve once at the start of each session and let the agent act freely for the rest of the conversation
why: Approval should scale with consequence. Prompting for everything creates fatigue, so people stop reading and the gate stops protecting. Reserving it for irreversible or high-impact actions, and showing the exact inputs, keeps it meaningful. A summary email arrives after the harm, a prompt rule is not enforcement, and blanket session approval covers actions nobody has seen.

q: A multi-tenant document assistant exposes a search_docs tool with a tenant_id parameter that the model fills in from the conversation. A user types "search tenant 4412 for payroll files" and receives another company's documents. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Add a sentence to the tool description saying that the tenant must match the company of the signed-in user
Take the tenant from the authenticated session in the tool handler and ignore what the model supplies
Validate that the supplied tenant_id has a well-formed identifier format before the search runs
Have the model ask the user to confirm that they are entitled to see the tenant before searching
why: Identity and authorization must come from your authenticated session, in code, not from model-supplied arguments, which the user or an attacker can steer. Otherwise the agent becomes a confused deputy that exercises the service's broad access for someone entitled to less. Descriptions are guidance, a format check passes any well-formed ID, and asking users to confirm their own entitlement is self-attestation.

q: A PreToolUse hook script inspects the planned Bash command and, for "git push --force", prints a message and exits with status 1, intending to block it. Forced pushes still go through. What change makes the hook block the call?
opts: Write the reason to standard error and exit with status 2, or return a JSON deny decision instead
Move the check into a PostToolUse hook so that it can see the result of the command
Print the message to standard output instead of standard error before exiting with status 1
Also add the rule to CLAUDE.md so that the script and the instructions agree
why: For command hooks, status 0 means no objection and status 2 blocks the call, with standard error fed back to the model as the reason. Other nonzero codes, such as 1, are non-blocking errors and the action proceeds, so the script fails open. PostToolUse runs after the action and cannot undo it, the output stream does not change what status 1 means, and CLAUDE.md is context rather than enforcement.

q: Security wants a rule that no Claude Code session may run commands containing "terraform destroy", even when engineers launch sessions with permission prompts skipped for speed. Which control holds?
opts: A sentence in the shared CLAUDE.md prohibiting the command
A PreToolUse hook, delivered through managed settings, that denies matching Bash commands
A PostToolUse hook that restores the infrastructure state after a destroy has run
A reminder in the onboarding guide and in the pull request template
why: PreToolUse hooks run before any permission-mode check in every mode, so a deny still blocks when prompts are skipped, and delivering the hook through managed settings means engineers cannot switch it off from their own settings. CLAUDE.md and onboarding text are guidance, and a PostToolUse hook runs after the damage and cannot undo it.

q: A company runs its Claude-based service on Kubernetes in a major cloud. Security policy forbids long-lived secrets in the cluster, and an audit flagged the static API key stored in a Kubernetes secret. Which approach BEST meets the policy?
opts: Keep the static key in the cluster but rotate it monthly with a scheduled job and an audit reminder
Base64-encode the key in the manifest so that it is no longer stored in clear text in the repository
Give every developer a personal key and have the service use the key of whoever deployed it most recently
Use Workload Identity Federation: exchange the pod identity token for short-lived Claude API tokens
why: Federation replaces a stored key with a short-lived token exchanged from an identity the platform already issues, so there is nothing long-lived to leak or rotate (its strength depends on the identity provider setup). Monthly rotation still leaves a static secret in the cluster, base64 is encoding rather than protection, and a personal key ties the service to one person's access and lifetime.

q: An engineer accidentally pushes an API key to a public repository and notices a few minutes later. What should happen FIRST?
opts: Rewrite the repository history to remove the commit and watch whether the key is misused afterwards
Leave the key active until it expires, since expiry already limits the exposure to a short window
Disable or delete the key in the Console so it stops working, then issue a replacement
Message the team to avoid using that key while the repository is cleaned up and the history is rewritten
why: A published key must be assumed compromised the moment it is public, so revocation comes first (disable is reversible, delete is permanent), followed by a replacement, a review of usage and a root-cause fix such as secret scanning. Cleaning history does not un-leak copies that already exist, waiting for expiry leaves the key usable meanwhile, and asking colleagues to avoid it does nothing about an attacker.

q: A research agent browses the web and summarizes pages for users. Which THREE measures reduce the damage from indirect prompt injection? (Choose three.)
opts: Return page text inside tool results, labeled with its source, under a system prompt policy that treats it as data
Give the agent only read-only tools and run it in a sandbox with a network allowlist
Place the fetched text in the system prompt so that the model weighs it carefully
Ask users to avoid submitting URLs whose pages might contain malicious text
Test the agent before launch with pages that deliberately contain injected instructions
why: Isolating and labeling third-party content, limiting what a fooled agent can do, and red-teaming with hostile pages are all parts of a layered defense. The system prompt carries the highest authority, so fetched text never belongs there, and asking users to avoid risky pages is not a control: the attacker plants the text, not the user.

q: An agent that processes confidential documents also has outbound network access. Which TWO controls best limit the damage if an injected instruction turns it against you? (Choose two.)
opts: A system prompt line telling the agent never to send data to unknown domains
An egress allowlist enforced by a proxy or firewall outside the agent's environment
A higher effort setting so that the agent reasons carefully about every outbound request
Credentials kept outside the agent's boundary, with a proxy that injects them into approved requests
A log of the agent's outbound requests that the agent itself is able to edit
why: Network controls outside the agent stop exfiltration even when the agent has been fooled, and a credential proxy means there is no secret for it to leak while also giving you a place to enforce the allowlist. A prompt line is guidance, effort is a cost and quality setting, and a log the agent can edit cannot be trusted to detect anything.

q: Which TWO practices limit the damage if a Claude API key leaks? (Choose two.)
opts: Create keys with an expiration suited to their purpose and rotate them on a schedule
Share one production key across all services so that only a single key has to be tracked
Use separate keys scoped to separate workspaces for development, staging and production
Embed the key in client-side code so that it can be replaced without a server deployment
Keep the key in a private repository so that only employees can read it
why: Expiry and rotation cap how long a stolen key works, and per-environment, workspace-scoped keys keep a leak in development from exposing production. A single shared key widens the blast radius, client-side code exposes the key to every user, and a private repository still spreads the secret to everyone with access and into history.

q: A security team wants to detect misuse of its Claude credentials and agent actions. Which TWO practices support authorized access monitoring? (Choose two.)
opts: Give all services one shared key so that the usage dashboard has a single line to watch
Give each workload its own identity-backed key so that usage can be attributed and unusual patterns stand out
Turn off request logging in the tool layer to avoid storing sensitive inputs
Write each tool call, its caller identity and its outcome to a log that the agent cannot modify, and review it for anomalies
Rely on end users to report anything that looks wrong
why: Attribution and tamper-resistant records are what make monitoring possible: separate identities show who or what is acting, and an audit log the agent cannot edit lets you reconstruct events and spot odd behavior. A shared key hides which workload is responsible, disabling logging removes the evidence (keep secrets and unnecessary personal data out of the log instead), and user reports are not systematic monitoring.

q: No system prompt wording can guarantee that its contents stay hidden, so a system prompt should never contain secrets.
opts: True
False
why: A model can be induced to repeat text it can see. Keep credentials and sensitive logic in server-side code, and treat output monitoring as a way to catch leaks rather than a guarantee against them.

q: Prompt injection can only come from the typed input of the application's own end users.
opts: True
False
why: Indirect injection arrives through content the model reads on a user's behalf, such as web pages, emails, documents and tool results, where the user is honest and an attacker has planted the text.

q: A zero data retention arrangement covers the Message Batches API and the Files API in the same way that it covers standard Messages API calls.
opts: True
False
why: Stateful features such as batch jobs and stored files are not ZDR-eligible; using them is a choice to step outside the arrangement for that data. Check the feature eligibility table before designing a regulated workflow.

q: A personal API key keeps working after its owner is removed from the organization.
opts: True
False
why: Personal keys act as the user and are archived when that person leaves the organization, which is why shared or unattended workloads should use a service account key or federation instead.

q: A PostToolUse hook can undo a tool action that has already run, so it prevents destructive commands as well as a PreToolUse hook does.
opts: True
False
why: PostToolUse fires after the tool has succeeded and cannot reverse it. To prevent an action, deny it in a PreToolUse hook (or with a deny rule); use PostToolUse for follow-up work such as formatting or logging.

q: An inventory assistant has two tools: lookup_item (finds one item by SKU and returns stock and location) and search_items (full-text search over names, returning up to 20 matches with their SKUs). Both are described only as "Gets inventory information," and the model often calls the wrong one. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Merge them into one tool named inventory that accepts a single free-text query parameter
Force one tool on every request with tool_choice and let application code decide which one to use
Rewrite each description: what the tool does, when to use it instead of the other, its parameters and its result
Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing which tool to prefer for each kind of question
why: The description is the most influential input to tool selection. Differentiating the two by when to use each, with parameters and results spelled out, resolves the ambiguity where the model reads it. A free-text merge hides a real difference between the tools, forced tool choice removes the model's judgment (and is rejected on the newest models), and prompt-level guidance duplicates what belongs with the tool and drifts away from it.

q: A booking tool returns the text "error" when it is given a date in the past. The model retries the same call three times and then apologizes to the user. Which change to the tool is BEST?
opts: Flag the result as an error with a message such as "start_date must be in the future; today is 2026-10-15"
Raise an exception in the harness so that the whole conversation ends and the user can start again with a new request
Return an empty result that looks successful so that the model is not distracted by a failure
Increase the SDK's automatic retry count so that more attempts are made before giving up
why: A failed call should come back with the error flag set and say what went wrong and what to try, so the model can correct the argument itself. Ending the run wastes the chance to recover, an empty success misreports the outcome, and SDK retries address transient network and server failures, not invalid arguments.

q: In a manual tool loop, Claude requests a send_email tool call. The harness shows the draft to a manager, who declines it. What should the harness send back to the model?
opts: Nothing at all: end the conversation, because a call that was declined cannot be answered and the user already knows
A new assistant message that apologizes to the user on the model's behalf
An ordinary user text message with no tool_result, since the tool never ran
A tool_result for that tool_use ID flagged as an error, saying that the person declined and why
why: Every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result in the next user message, even when the action is refused. An error result that says the person declined lets the model change course or explain. Ending the run, writing assistant text on the model's behalf, or omitting the result leaves the exchange malformed or the model without information.

q: A product assistant needs live web lookups and must also read order totals from the company's internal billing service. The team wants to write as little integration code as possible. Which tool setup is BEST?
opts: The web search server tool for both needs, configured with the billing service's internal URL
The web search server tool for lookups, plus a custom client tool whose handler calls the billing service
Custom client tools for both, with a web scraping library and a result parser that you write and maintain for lookups
No tools: paste the billing totals into the system prompt and rely on training data for the web
why: Server-executed tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure, which cannot reach your private network, but they spare you from building web search. Internal systems need a client tool (or an MCP server) whose handler you own. Rebuilding search adds code for no benefit, and pasted totals go stale while training data is not live.

q: An agent is connected to five MCP servers and sees about 60 tool definitions that together use tens of thousands of tokens on every request. Most tasks need only three or four of them, and the model sometimes picks the wrong one. What is the BEST change?
opts: Shorten every description to a few words so that all 60 definitions take up much less space
Set tool_choice to any so that the model must commit to a tool at the first step
Use tool search with deferred loading, so definitions are loaded only when the model discovers them
Cache the tool definitions so that they no longer count against the window when the model chooses between tools
why: Tool search keeps most definitions out of the prompt until the model searches for them, which cuts context cost and improves selection in large catalogs (worth considering from roughly 20 tools). Terse descriptions make choosing harder, forcing a tool call does not help pick the right one, and caching lowers the price without reducing the number of choices the model must weigh.

q: An expense agent must check 150 receipts against a vendor API. Each call returns about 2,000 tokens, the model makes 150 round trips, and the conversation soon overflows. Which technique BEST addresses the cause?
opts: Programmatic tool calling, so a script loops over the receipts and returns only a short summary
Tool search, so that the vendor tool's definition is loaded only when it is needed and not on every request
Prompt caching, so that the repeated results are billed at the lower cache rate
A larger max_tokens value so that the model can finish writing out all 150 calls
why: The bulk comes from intermediate tool results and round trips. Running the loop in code inside the code execution sandbox keeps those results out of the model's context and returns only what the next decision needs. Tool search targets large catalogs of definitions, caching changes the price rather than the space used, and max_tokens caps a single reply.

q: A classification service sets tool_choice to force a call to classify_ticket. After the team switches to Claude Sonnet 5.5, every request fails with a 400 error, yet the service still needs a label from a fixed set on every call. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Retry each failed request until the API accepts the forced tool choice
Request the label with structured outputs, using a schema whose field is an enum of the allowed labels
Drop the schema and parse the label out of the model's prose answer with a regular expression and a table of synonyms
Move back to an older model generation solely to keep the forced tool choice working
why: Forced tool choice is not supported on the newest models, so retrying cannot succeed. Structured outputs constrain the reply to a schema, so the label comes from your closed set without forcing a tool (compare labels case-insensitively, because the capitalization of enum values is not guaranteed). Regex over prose is the fragile pattern a schema replaces, and a downgrade trades current capabilities away to avoid a design change.

q: A project's CLAUDE.md includes a 400-word quarterly-close procedure that matters for a few tasks a month. It loads into every session and makes the file long. Where should this procedure move?
opts: A hook that prints the whole procedure at the start of every session
The system prompt of every API call the team makes, so that it is applied consistently
A skill, so that only its short description stays in context and the steps load when the task matches
An MCP server that serves the procedure through a tool the model calls at the start of every task
why: A skill uses progressive disclosure: its name and description are always available, the body loads when the task matches, and supporting files load on demand. CLAUDE.md is for facts that apply to nearly every session. A hook that prints the text, a system prompt and an MCP tool called on every task would each put the procedure back in context all the time, or add moving parts for no gain.

q: A team connected an MCP server for its issue tracker. Claude can now create and update issues, but it applies labels and templates inconsistently with the team's conventions. What addition is BEST?
opts: A skill that documents the team's labeling and template conventions and when to use each tool
A second MCP server that exposes the same issue-tracker tools under different names
A hook that prints a reminder after every tool call, whether or not it concerns issues
A larger model tier, since inconsistent behavior means the current model lacks capability
why: The server supplies the connection; what is missing is know-how about the team's way of using it, which is what a skill packages and loads when relevant. Another server duplicates the capability, a reminder after every call is noise, and the model is not the problem when the conventions were never written down.

q: One internal web app needs Claude to call a small function that computes shipping quotes from the app's own database. No other application will use it. Which approach is BEST?
opts: A standalone MCP server with its own deployment, authentication and release process
A skill that explains the quote formula so that the model can work the quotes out itself
A built-in tool, since built-in tools can query any application's database
A custom tool in the app's tool list, whose handler calls the function in the same codebase
why: For logic that belongs to one application, a custom tool is the simplest and cheapest option: a schema plus a handler. A protocol server pays off when several clients need the capability or it must be maintained independently, so building one here adds operations work for no reuse. A skill cannot read the database, and built-in tools do not reach arbitrary application data.

q: A team plans to give Claude Code thirty skills for different procedures and worries that they will consume the context window in every session. Which statement is accurate?
opts: All thirty skill bodies load at session start, so the team should keep the total under a few hundred words and drop the rest
Only each skill's short name and description stays in context, and a skill's full instructions load when it is used
Skills load only when a person types their slash command, so the model can never use one on its own
Each skill runs as a background process whose output is appended to every reply
why: Skills use progressive disclosure, which is why a large library is cheap: descriptions are always visible so the model knows what exists, bodies load on demand, and supporting files load only when referenced. Skills can also be invoked by the model when a task matches (unless that is switched off for a skill), and they are instructions, not background processes.

q: Three teams each copied the same two skills, a formatting hook and an MCP server entry into their repositories, and the copies are drifting apart. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Merge the three repositories into one monorepo so that there is only a single copy to keep
Move all of the content into each repository's CLAUDE.md, which every session loads automatically
Package it as a plugin in a marketplace and have each repository install it and update it deliberately
Ask each team to compare its copy with the others at the start of every quarter
why: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP configuration into one versioned unit that can be installed in many repositories. CLAUDE.md can carry instructions but not hooks or server definitions, merging repositories is a large organizational change for a packaging problem, and a manual quarterly comparison is the process that is already failing.

q: A coding agent defines its own edit_file tool with a home-made schema for describing text replacements. The model often produces malformed edits. Which change is MOST likely to help?
opts: Use Anthropic's text editor tool, whose schema the models were trained on, with your own handler
Turn the tool into a server-executed tool so that Anthropic runs the edits for you
Paste the whole file into the tool description so that the model has more context about it before it edits
Make the schema accept one free-form string so that the model has more flexibility
why: Anthropic-schema tools such as the text editor, bash and memory have definitions the models were trained on, so calls tend to be more reliable than with an equivalent home-made schema, but your own code still executes them. They are client tools, not server tools. Pasting file contents bloats the description and free-form strings remove the structure that makes an edit unambiguous.

q: A developer's local MCP server passes its unit tests, but a host application that launches it as a subprocess reports parse errors on startup. The server prints a banner and debug lines with print(). What is the correct fix?
opts: Switch the server to Streamable HTTP, because the stdio transport cannot carry any log output
Print a blank line before each banner so that the client can skip over the extra text
Increase the host's startup timeout so that the extra lines are ignored while it waits
Send logging and diagnostics to standard error, and keep standard output for protocol messages only
why: Over stdio, standard output carries newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages and nothing else; the server may write logs to standard error. A stray print corrupts the stream. The remote transport is not needed, a blank line is still invalid output, and a longer timeout does not change what is on the stream.

q: An MCP tool that books meeting rooms receives a start time in the wrong format. The server currently answers with a JSON-RPC error and a generic message, and the model cannot recover. Which design lets the model self-correct?
opts: Keep the protocol error and add a table of numeric error codes to the server documentation
Return a normal result with the error flag set and a message naming the expected format and an example
Coerce any malformed time to the nearest valid time and book the room without telling anyone, so the call always succeeds
Return an empty successful result and log the problem for an administrator to read later
why: Protocol errors cover malformed requests and unknown tools. A failure inside the tool, such as bad input, a business rule or a backend outage, should be reported in the result with isError set and an actionable message, so the model can fix its arguments and retry. Documentation is not seen by the model, silent coercion books the wrong time, and an empty success hides the failure.

q: A server author must expose three things: a function that creates tickets, a read-only file holding the current database schema, and a weekly-report template that users pick from a menu. Which mapping to MCP primitives is correct?
opts: A prompt for the ticket function, a tool for the schema file and a resource for the report template
A resource for the ticket function, a prompt for the schema file and a tool for the report template
A tool for the ticket function, a resource for the schema file and a prompt for the report template
Tools for all three, since only tools can be listed and invoked by a client
why: Tools are model-controlled functions that act, resources are read-only context that the application attaches, and prompts are templates a person selects deliberately. The other mappings put an action behind a read-only primitive or make the model choose a human-facing template, and clients can list resources and prompts as well as tools.

q: A developer wants the Messages API's MCP connector to use an MCP server that runs on their laptop over stdio and exposes both tools and resources. The request fails. Which statement explains why and points to the right alternative?
opts: The connector accepts stdio servers only when they are under 1 MB, so the server has to be compressed and uploaded to the platform first
The connector requires every server to be registered in the Claude Console before a request is allowed to name it
The connector works with local servers too, but only when the request sets a stdio transport flag on the server
The connector reaches only public HTTP servers and only tools; local servers need Claude Code, the Agent SDK or your own client
why: The Messages API connector is a beta feature that connects to remote servers over HTTP that are reachable from the internet, and it supports tool calls only, not resources or prompts. A subprocess server on a laptop needs a client that can launch it, such as Claude Code, the Agent SDK or a client you write. The other statements describe limits and flags that do not exist.

q: Which THREE belong in a well-written tool description? (Choose three.)
opts: When the tool should be used and when it should not
What each parameter means, including its expected format
The credentials the handler uses to authenticate to the backend service
What the result contains and any important limits, such as fields it leaves out
A parameter asking the model to write out its step-by-step reasoning for the call
why: A description is the model's manual for the tool: purpose, when to use it, parameters, and results with their caveats. Credentials never belong in text the model can see, so handlers read them from the environment or a secret store, and a parameter that asks for step-by-step reasoning can trigger a refusal; ask for a short explanation or the supporting evidence instead.

q: A team is designing tools for GitHub and Slack integrations. Which TWO design choices follow good practice? (Choose two.)
opts: Expose one generic call_api tool that accepts any URL, method and body
Prefix tool names with the service, such as github_list_prs and slack_send_message
Group closely related pull-request operations into one tool with an action parameter
Give every tool the same short description so that the model treats them consistently
Return the full raw API response from every tool so that no information is lost
why: Namespacing keeps similar tools from different systems unambiguous as the catalog grows, and consolidating related operations gives the model fewer, clearer choices. A catch-all tool removes the structure that guides and limits calls (and makes permissioning hard), identical descriptions make selection impossible, and raw responses bury the few fields that matter.

q: A team runs an MCP server on developers' machines over Streamable HTTP. Which TWO protections does the specification call for? (Choose two.)
opts: Validate the Origin header on incoming connections to defend against DNS rebinding
Skip authentication, because only processes on the same machine can reach a local server
Expose the server on all network interfaces so that teammates can connect for pair debugging
Bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than to all interfaces when the server runs locally
Accept any Origin value so that browser-based clients are never blocked
why: Servers must validate the Origin header (answering an invalid one with 403) and, when run locally, should bind only to localhost; they should also authenticate connections. Without these protections, a malicious web page can use DNS rebinding to talk to a server on the developer's machine. Skipping authentication, binding to every interface and accepting any Origin each reopen that path.

q: Which THREE pairings of a need and an extension mechanism are right? (Choose three.)
opts: A check that must run after every file edit, with no exceptions: a hook
A convention that applies in nearly every session, such as the test command: a skill the model must choose to invoke
A procedure the team keeps pasting into chat: a skill
A noisy investigation that would flood the main conversation: a note in CLAUDE.md
Reading and updating tickets in a SaaS tool that Claude cannot reach: an MCP server
why: Guaranteed, every-time behavior belongs in a hook because hooks are executed, not suggested. Reusable procedures belong in skills, and a connection to an outside system belongs in an MCP server. Facts that apply to almost every session belong in CLAUDE.md rather than in something the model must decide to invoke, and a noisy investigation belongs in a subagent with its own context.

q: Strict tool use makes tool arguments conform to the schema, but a conforming argument can still be the wrong value.
opts: True
False
why: Strict mode constrains decoding so field names and types are valid. It cannot know whether the order ID exists or the amount is right, so the dispatcher still validates and authorizes every call.

q: When Claude uses a server-executed tool such as web search, your code must build a tool_result block for each search it makes.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic runs server tools and returns their results in the same response, so there is no tool_result for you to build. You only handle the case where the loop pauses (pause_turn) or a client tool is called alongside.

q: A one-phrase description is sufficient for a tool as long as the tool's name is clear.
opts: True
False
why: The description is the most influential factor in tool performance. A name cannot say when to use the tool, what each parameter expects or what comes back, so aim for several sentences.

q: Tool descriptions and annotations from an MCP server you do not control should be treated as untrusted input.
opts: True
False
why: A server's descriptions are text the model will read, so a malicious or compromised server can use them to steer it. Clients should confirm sensitive operations, show inputs to the user and validate results.

q: The older HTTP+SSE transport for MCP has been deprecated in favor of Streamable HTTP.
opts: True
False

q: A skill and an MCP server solve the same problem, so a team should choose one or the other.

False
why: An MCP server provides a connection to tools and data; a skill teaches how and when to use them. They are complementary, and many teams use both.

q: A built-in tool can be used without building it, but it does not give Claude access to arbitrary internal systems.
